titulo: proxy_bypass_registry uses unanchored re.match (Windows proxy bypass)
corpo: This was discussed here multiple times in the past so I'm opening it as a public bug report.  `src/requests/utils.py`, `proxy_bypass_registry` (main, 2.34.2):  ```python if re.match(test, host, re.I):   # start-anchored only     return True ```  re.match anchors only the start, so ProxyOverride=google.com matches google.com.evil.com and bypasses the proxy for it — an attacker-influenced hostname can escape a proxy meant to inspect traffic.  Diverges from CPython: this is a copy of CPython's old code. CPython now matches with fnmatch (anchored both ends, wildcards preserved). Verified on 3.14: - `fnmatch("google.com.evil.com", "google.com")` → False (requests returns True) - `fnmatch("a.example.net", "*.example.net")` → True  Fix: use fnmatch(host, test) to match CPython, or minimally anchor: re.match(test + r"\Z", host, re.I).

titulo: Docstring examples in `from_key_val_list` show the pre-3.12 OrderedDict repr
corpo: `src/requests/utils.py`'s `from_key_val_list` docstring shows:      >>> from_key_val_list([('key', 'val')])     OrderedDict([('key', 'val')])  Since Python 3.12, `collections.OrderedDict.__repr__` uses the regular dict form ([cpython gh-101446](https://github.com/python/cpython/issues/101446)), so on any currently supported Python this actually prints:      OrderedDict({'key': 'val'})  Reproducer (Python 3.13.5, requests 2.34.2):  ``` >>> from requests.utils import from_key_val_list >>> from_key_val_list([('key', 'val')]) OrderedDict({'key': 'val'}) >>> from_key_val_list({'key': 'val'}) OrderedDict({'key': 'val'}) ```  The `ValueError` example in the same docstring is still accurate. Both stale occurrences are on lines 351 and 357, and a grep of the rest of the package found no others.  I have a two-line fix ready on a fork and would be glad to open a pull request if that's welcome. (The compare page says PRs are limited to collaborators, hence this issue.)

titulo: API-provided proxies are silently overridden by environment variables; no per-request opt-out
corpo: Summary Requests automatically uses environment proxies from HTTP_PROXY, HTTPS_PROXY, etc. There is currently no clean per-request way to disable this behavior. The only reliable workaround is to create a Session and set ```session.trust_env = False.```  Current behavior When proxy-related environment variables are present, a simple request such as: ``` requests.get(url, proxies={}) ``` still uses the environment proxy. Passing an empty proxies dict does not mean “disable all proxies”; it means “no API-level proxy was provided”, so environment proxies are merged in by Session.merge_environment_settings() when trust_env is True.  To actually bypass environment proxies, users must write:  ``` session = requests.Session() session.trust_env = False session.get(url) ``` They cannot write:  ``` requests.get(url, trust_env=False) ``` Expected behavior I would like one of the following: `proxies={}` (or explicit None values) to reliably disable all proxies for that request, including environment proxies; or`trust_env `to be accepted as a per-request argument, e.g. `requests.get(url, trust_env=False)`.  Why this matters Simple scripts and library wrappers cannot easily switch to a Session.  CI / container environments often set `HTTP_PROXY `/ `HTTPS_PROXY `globally.  Some requests need to use the system proxy while others need to bypass it.  Forcing every caller to create and configure a Session adds unnecessary boilerplate.  Recent proxy-related changes, such as stricter proxy URL parsing in 2.32.0+, make this behavior more visible and harder to work around.  Workaround Currently the only reliable workaround is:  ``` session = requests.Session() session.trust_env = False response = session.get(url) ``` This works, but it is not convenient and cannot be applied directly to top-level requests.get() / requests.post() calls.  Proposed API Allow `trust_env `to be passed per request:  ``` requests.get(url, trust_env=False) ``` Alternatively, define `proxies={} `as an explicit opt-out from all environment proxies.

titulo: OpenSSL 4 removed built-in logic for SKID and AKID
corpo: <!-- Summary. -->  The openssl command used to have built-in logic to automaticaly add subjectKeyIdentifier and authorityKeyIdentifier to created certificates. This logic vanished in OpenSSL 4.0 and the extensions are missing.      Python 3.13+ uses VERIFY_X509_STRICT to verify the certificate. Missing those attributes is an error.  ## Expected Result  A certificated with SKID and AKID.  ## Actual Result  No SKID and AKID.  ## Reproduction Steps  ``` $ openssl version OpenSSL 4.0.2 25 Aug 2026 (Library: OpenSSL 4.0.2 25 Aug 2026) for cert in expired mtls valid/server ; do make -C  tests/certs/$cert clean all; done pytest -v tests/test_requests.py ``` And then somewhere appears ```  error = SSLError(SSLCertVerificationError(1, '[SSL: CERTIFICATE_VERIFY_FAILED] certificate verify failed: Missing Authority Key Identifier (_ssl.c:1082)'))  _pool = <urllib3.connectionpool.HTTPSConnectionPool object at 0x7f0a6d92a2c0>  _stacktrace = <traceback object at 0x7f0a6dfa7a80> ....  FAILED tests/test_requests.py::TestPreparingURLs::test_different_connection_pool_for_tls_settings_verify_bundle_unexpired_cert ```  I prepared https://github.com/sebastianas/requests/commit/339333739074118a93a9f496981b394e94bc1690 as a fix but can't open a pull request. titulo: Proposed fix for #5888: preserve manually-set Proxy-Authorization on initial request
corpo: Hi maintainers 👋  I prepared a minimal fix proposal for issue #5888 and would appreciate your review/feedback.  ## Problem statement  In the current behavior discussed in #5888, a manually-set `Proxy-Authorization` header may be removed too aggressively, including the initial request path in some flows.  ## Proposed behavior  - Preserve manually-set `Proxy-Authorization` on the **initial request** path. - Keep stripping behavior on **redirect/proxy-change** paths where rebuilding proxy auth is expected.  ## Implementation scope  I kept the patch intentionally small and focused:  - `requests/sessions.py` - `tests/test_5888_regression.py` (new regression tests)  ## What tests cover  - initial non-redirect request preserves manually-set `Proxy-Authorization` - redirect/proxy-change path strips header as expected - no regression in related auth/header interaction  ## Patch branch  I cannot open a direct PR due to repository permission restrictions, so I’m sharing the branch here:  - Fork: `aj-aura/requests` - Branch: `fix/proxy-auth-header-5888` - Compare link:   https://github.com/psf/requests/compare/main...aj-aura:requests:fix/proxy-auth-header-5888?expand=1  If this direction looks good, I can adjust the patch immediately based on maintainer guidance.  Thanks!

titulo: Discrepancy in status_codes.py: 102 mapped to "early-hints" instead of 103
corpo: In `src/requests/status_codes.py`, `"early-hints"` is currently associated with status code `102` rather than `103`. Furthermore, the alias was defined only as a hyphenated string, preventing dot-attribute access (`requests.codes.early_hints`). ## Expected Result - `requests.codes.processing` and `requests.codes.get("processing")` resolve to `102` (RFC 9110 §15.2.3 / RFC 2518). - `requests.codes.early_hints`, `requests.codes.EARLY_HINTS`, and `requests.codes.get("early-hints")` resolve to `103` (RFC 9110 §15.2.4 / RFC 8297). ## Actual Result - `requests.codes.get("early-hints")` returns `102`. - `requests.codes.early_hints` raises `AttributeError: 'LookupDict' object has no attribute 'early_hints'`.  ## Reproduction Steps  ```python import requests # "early-hints" incorrectly returns 102 assert requests.codes.get("early-hints") == 102  # Should be 103 # Attribute access fails due to hyphenated definition try:     _ = requests.codes.early_hints except AttributeError as e:     print(f"AttributeError: {e}")  ```  ## System Information      $ python -m requests.help  ```json {   "chardet": {     "version": null   },   "charset_normalizer": {     "version": "3.5.1"   },   "cryptography": {     "version": ""   },   "idna": {     "version": "3.18"   },   "implementation": {     "name": "CPython",     "version": "3.13.15"   },   "platform": {     "release": "11",     "system": "Windows"   },   "pyOpenSSL": {     "openssl_version": "",     "version": null   },   "requests": {     "version": "2.34.2"   },   "system_ssl": {     "version": "30000150"   },   "urllib3": {     "version": "2.7.0"   },   "using_charset_normalizer": true,   "using_pyopenssl": false }  ```  Note: A ready fix and regression tests have been prepared on fork branch [`Shaivarth:fix-rfc9110-status-codes`](https://github.com/Shaivarth/requests/tree/fix-rfc9110-status-codes) (commit [`a2480570`](https://github.com/Shaivarth/requests/commit/a2480570)).   <!-- This command is only available on Requests v2.16.4 and greater. titulo: Drop the versionless `License ::` classifier now that `license` is a valid SPDX expression
corpo: > This issue is part of a larger batch of similar-scoped issues we distribute in the context of our internal vulnerability and dependency tracking activities. The batch covers multiple projects, this is only one of them. The goal is to rise awareness and trigger/initiate the change towards clean project metadata in projects we depend on.  ## Summary  This project already declares a valid SPDX license id/expression in its packaging metadata (`License: Apache-2.0` in the built METADATA), but the deprecated classifier `License :: OSI Approved :: Apache Software License` is still present. That classifier has no version and [PEP 639](https://peps.python.org/pep-0639/)-aware SBOM tooling like [cyclonedx-bom](https://pypi.org/project/cyclonedx-bom/) can't map it to an SPDX id, so it falls back to emitting the raw classifier text as a free-text license name. This free-text field is just noise and causes downstream tooling to flag this project as non-SPDX-compliant.  ## Suggested fix  Remove the redundant `License :: OSI Approved :: Apache Software License` from `classifiers` in the packaging config. No change to the `license` field is needed.  ## How to reproduce  ```bash uv tool install cyclonedx-bom uv venv .venv-repro uv pip install --python .venv-repro/bin/python requests cyclonedx-py environment .venv-repro -o sbom.cdx.json ```  ... and then check the `.licenses` property of the component. There should only something like:  ```json // This is how it should look like ...     "license": {         "acknowledgement": "declared",         "id": "<VALID SPDX IDENTIFIER>"     } ... ```  and _not_:  ```json // This is how it should not look like ...     "license": {        "acknowledgement": "declared",        "name": "<CLASSIFIER TAKEN FROM METADATA"     } ... ```  I'm happy to provide a PR to resolve this timely after approval!

titulo: SSRF: Unrestricted redirect following allows internal network access
corpo: ## Summary  get_redirect_target() and resolve_redirects() in sessions.py follow redirects to any URL without validating the target, allowing SSRF to internal IPs/cloud metadata endpoints.  ## Vulnerability  Location: src/requests/sessions.py:134  No validation on redirect targets — can redirect to: - localhost (127.0.0.0/8) - RFC 1918 networks (10.x, 172.16-31.x, 192.168.x) - Cloud metadata endpoints (169.254.169.254)  ## Impact - Internal network probing - Cloud metadata exfiltration - Access to internal services  ## Fix Add SSRF protection to redirect resolution: - Validate redirect target host IP - Block private/loopback/link-local/multicast IPs - Add optional allow-list for trusted hosts

titulo: Cookies are not sent when the URL contains credentials
corpo: `requests` extracts credentials embedded in a URL and sends them as an `Authorization` header, but the same URL then matches no cookie in the jar, so cookies are silently omitted.  ## Expected Result  A cookie scoped to `127.0.0.1` is sent for `http://user:pw@127.0.0.1:PORT/`, just as it is for `http://127.0.0.1:PORT/`. The userinfo component is not part of the host (RFC 3986 §3.2), and cookie matching is on the host (RFC 6265).  ## Actual Result  The `Authorization` header is sent, but `Cookie` is omitted:  ``` without credentials  Authorization=None                  Cookie='sid=secret' with credentials     Authorization='Basic dXNlcjpwdw=='  Cookie=None ```  The credentials are honoured for authentication, so the URL form is clearly supported, but cookie matching on that same URL fails. No error or warning is raised.  ## Reproduction Steps  Run a local HTTP server that records the `Authorization` and `Cookie` request headers it receives. Create a `Session` and set a cookie on it scoped to `domain="127.0.0.1"`, `path="/"`. Issue two GETs against the server: one to `http://127.0.0.1:PORT/`, and one to `http://user:pw@127.0.0.1:PORT/`. The first arrives with the `Cookie` header set and no `Authorization`; the second arrives with `Authorization` set and no `Cookie`.  ## System Information  ```json {   "chardet": {"version": null},   "charset_normalizer": {"version": "3.5.1"},   "cryptography": {"version": ""},   "idna": {"version": "3.18"},   "implementation": {"name": "CPython", "version": "3.14.7"},   "platform": {"release": "25.6.0", "system": "Darwin"},   "pyOpenSSL": {"openssl_version": "", "version": null},   "requests": {"version": "2.34.2"},   "system_ssl": {"version": "30600030"},   "urllib3": {"version": "2.7.0"},   "using_charset_normalizer": true,   "using_pyopenssl": false } ```

titulo: LookupDict does not implement full contract of the dict class
corpo:
## Problem Description

The `LookupDict` class in `src/requests/structures.py` subclasses `dict` but does not properly implement the full contract of the `dict` class. Specifically:

1. `__getitem__` and `__getattr__` methods read from `self.__dict__` (plain attribute storage) rather than the actual dict storage
2. All inherited `dict` methods (`__setitem__`, `keys()`, `values()`, `items()`, `get()` via the base class, `in`/`__contains__`, etc.) operate on the *actual* dict storage
3. This creates two disconnected stores, leading to inconsistent behavior

## Reproduction

```python
from requests.status_codes import codes
list(codes.keys())        # returns [] — should include e.g. 'ok', 'not_found', ...
codes["my_code"] = 700    # succeeds (writes to dict storage)
codes["my_code"]          # returns None — should return 700 (read comes from __dict__)
```

## Expected Behavior

1. `list(codes.keys())` should reflect the actual status-code attributes set by `status_codes.py`'s `_init()`
2. `codes["ok"]` (dict-style) and `codes.ok` (attribute-style) should return the same value and stay consistent after either form of assignment
3. Unknown keys should still return `None` via `__getitem__`/`.get()` rather than raising `KeyError` (this is an intentional deviation from plain `dict`)

## Root Cause

In `src/requests/structures.py`, `LookupDict.__getitem__` returns `self.__dict__.get(key, None)` instead of using the dict's own storage.

## Impact

This inconsistency breaks the expected behavior of dict-like objects and prevents users from accessing status codes through standard dict methods.

## Fix

The fix should ensure that `__getitem__` and `__getattr__` methods synchronize with the actual dict storage, maintaining consistency between attribute and dictionary access patterns.

titulo: raise FileNotFoundError for missing TLS material
corpo: Would you accept a PR which changes the existing OSError for missing TLS material to FileNotFoundError?  e.g.:  ```             if conn.cert_file and not os.path.exists(conn.cert_file):                 raise OSError(                     f"Could not find the TLS certificate file, "                     f"invalid path: {conn.cert_file}"                 ) ```  becomes something like:  ```             if conn.cert_file and not os.path.exists(conn.cert_file):                 from errno import ENOENT                 raise FileNotFoundError(                     ENOENT,                     "Could not find the TLS certificate file, invalid path",                     str(conn.cert_file)                 ) ```  Our use case is that there are temporary conditions where the files don't exist and it'd be nicer to handle FileNotFoundError specifically and be able to compare the .filename attribute rather than the more general OSError and test str(excp).endswith(...).  As FileNotFoundError is a subclass of OSError existing try/excepts continue to work but it would change the string representation:  ``` >>> str(OSError("Could not find the TLS certificate file, invalid path: filename")) 'Could not find the TLS certificate file, invalid path: filename' >>> str(FileNotFoundError(errno.ENOENT, "Could not find the TLS certificate file, invalid path", "filename")) "[Errno 2] Could not find the TLS certificate file, invalid path: 'filename'" ```

titulo: `Session.get` docstring (added in #7429) is missing indentation, breaks Sphinx builds since v2.34.0
corpo: Since v2.34.0, `Session.get`'s docstring has a `:param params:` field whose continuation line isn't indented under the field. docutils treats the field list as ending mid-block, producing:  ``` WARNING: Field list ends without a blank line; unexpected unindent. [docutils] ```  Any Sphinx project that documents a subclass of `requests.Session` via `:inherited-members:` (or `automodapi`, etc.) now emits this warning. Projects building docs with `-W` / `fail_on_warning: true` (e.g. the Read the Docs default for many projects) fail outright.  ## Expected Result  `sphinx-build` renders `Session.get`'s docstring without docutils warnings, as was the case in v2.33.x.  ## Actual Result  ``` .../mymodule.py:docstring of requests.sessions.Session.get:5: WARNING: Field list ends without a blank line; unexpected unindent. [docutils] ```  ## Reproduction Steps  ```bash pip install 'requests==2.34.2' sphinx ```  `mymodule.py`: ```python from requests import Session  class MySession(Session):     pass ```  `conf.py`: ```python import os, sys sys.path.insert(0, os.path.abspath(".")) project = "repro" extensions = ["sphinx.ext.autodoc"] ```  `index.rst`: ```rst Repro =====  .. autoclass:: mymodule.MySession    :members:    :inherited-members: ```  Then: ```bash sphinx-build -b html -W . _build ```  Output: ``` .../mymodule.py:docstring of requests.sessions.Session.get:5: WARNING: Field list ends without a blank line; unexpected unindent. [docutils] build finished with problems, 1 warning (with warnings treated as errors). ```  ## System Information  ```json {   "requests": {"version": "2.34.2"},   "sphinx": {"version": "9.1.0"},   "docutils": {"version": "0.22.4"},   "implementation": {"name": "CPython", "version": "3.12.9"},   "platform": {"system": "Linux", "release": "6.17.0-20-generic"} } ```

titulo: typing.get_type_hints() fails on Response, PreparedRequest, and Request after 2.34.0
corpo: When preparing an update to 2.34.2 in Fedora Linux, I've found what I think is a bug in requests.  Since 2.34.0, calling typing.get_type_hints() on any of the three public model classes — or on any subclass of them — raises a NameError at runtime. The minimal reproducer is:  ```python import typing from requests import Response typing.get_type_hints(Response) # NameError: name 'RequestsCookieJar' is not defined ```  The same failure occurs for Request and PreparedRequest.  The 2.34.0 inline typing work introduced three things to models.py simultaneously that interact badly:  1. from `__future__` import annotations (PEP 563) — all annotations are now stored as strings instead of being evaluated eagerly. 2. Class-level annotations on the model classes that reference RequestsCookieJar, CookieJar, and HTTPAdapter:   - Request.cookies: RequestsCookieJar | CookieJar | dict[str, str] | None   - PreparedRequest._cookies: RequestsCookieJar | CookieJar | None   - Response.cookies: RequestsCookieJar   - Response.connection: HTTPAdapter 3. All three of those names (RequestsCookieJar, CookieJar, HTTPAdapter) are imported only inside if TYPE_CHECKING: — so they are absent from the module's runtime namespace.  When typing.get_type_hints() is called on any of these classes, it evaluates the stored annotation strings in requests.models's runtime globals. The names are not there, so a NameError is raised.  Note that sessions.py gets this right: it imports RequestsCookieJar unconditionally (not under TYPE_CHECKING), so get_type_hints(Session) works correctly. models.py needs to do the same.  Any library that subclasses Response, PreparedRequest, or Request and uses a tool that calls get_type_hints() — such as attrs.resolve_types() (used by cattrs for serialization) — is broken. A confirmed real-world case is requests-cache + requests-ratelimiter: caching any response fails with the NameError because cattrs calls resolve_types(CachedResponse) when building the unstructuring function for a class that inherits from Response.

titulo: Inline annotations in 2.34.0 cause mypy error for Request json payloads
corpo: requests version 2.34.0 added inline type annotations. This is causing some issues with mypy, specifically building a `Request` with a `json` argument.  The MR (https://github.com/psf/requests/pull/7272) that introduced the feature  notes that `mypy` support is not currently a goal, but I think it's worth sharing this issue.  ## Expected Result Passing a JSON-compatible dictionary to the `json` argument of `requests.Request` should type-check successfully.  For example, a value typed as:  ```python dict[str, None | bool | int | float | str] ``` or the narrower: ```python dict[str, str] ``` should be accepted as a valid JSON payload.  ## Actual Result `mypy` reports an incompatible argument type error when a dictionary is passed to the json argument.  ## Reproduction Steps Create a file named `test.py`:  ```python from requests import Request  payload: dict[str, str] = {"test": "test"}  request = Request(json=payload) ``` Then run mypy (used 2.1.0) against the python code: ```bash python -m mypy test.py test.py:5: error: Argument "json" to "Request" has incompatible type "dict[str, str]"; expected "JsonType"  [arg-type] test.py:5: note: "dict" is invariant -- see https://mypy.readthedocs.io/en/stable/common_issues.html#variance test.py:5: note: Consider using "Mapping" instead, which is covariant in the value type Found 1 error in 1 file (checked 1 source file) ```  ## System Information      $ python -m requests.help  ```json {   "chardet": {     "version": null   },   "charset_normalizer": {     "version": "3.4.7"   },   "cryptography": {     "version": ""   },   "idna": {     "version": "3.14"   },   "implementation": {     "name": "CPython",     "version": "3.13.13"   },   "platform": {     "release": "24.6.0",     "system": "Darwin"   },   "pyOpenSSL": {     "openssl_version": "",     "version": null   },   "requests": {     "version": "2.34.0"   },   "system_ssl": {     "version": "30600020"   },   "urllib3": {     "version": "2.7.0"   },   "using_charset_normalizer": true,   "using_pyopenssl": false } ```

titulo: `prepare_body` stream detection regression
corpo: <!-- Summary. --> Requests 2.34.0 changed the stream detection in PreparedRequest.prepare_body() from `hasattr(data, "__iter__")` to `isinstance(data, Iterable)`. This breaks file-like wrappers that expose `__iter__/read/tell/seek` via `__getattr__ delegation` (e.g. tqdm.wrapattr), because `isinstance(..., Iterable)` only checks the class MRO, not dynamic attribute delegation. As a result, `_body_position` is never recorded and the body cannot be rewound on 307/308 redirects. ## Expected Result  Upload completes successfully through the redirect, as it did in 2.33.1.  ## Actual Result  The redirected request sends an empty/consumed body. The server receives no data and the request times out: ``` requests.exceptions.ReadTimeout: HTTPSConnectionPool(...): Read timed out. (read timeout=30) ```  ## Reproduction Steps  ```python import os import requests from tqdm import tqdm  with open("testfile.txt", "wb") as f:     f.write(b"hello world " * 1000)  with open("testfile.txt", "rb") as f:     with tqdm.wrapattr(f, "read", total=os.path.getsize("testfile.txt")) as wrapped:         # Any endpoint that 307 redirects to a presigned S3 URL         requests.put("https://your-api.example.com/upload", data=wrapped, timeout=30)  ```  ## System Information      $ python -m requests.help  ```json {   "chardet": {     "version": null   },   "charset_normalizer": {     "version": "3.4.7"   },   "cryptography": {     "version": ""   },   "idna": {     "version": "3.13"   },   "implementation": {     "name": "CPython",     "version": "3.13.5"   },   "platform": {     "release": "24.6.0",     "system": "Darwin"   },   "pyOpenSSL": {     "openssl_version": "",     "version": null   },   "requests": {     "version": "2.34.0"   },   "system_ssl": {     "version": "30000120"   },   "urllib3": {     "version": "2.5.0"   },   "using_charset_normalizer": true,   "using_pyopenssl": false } ```  <!-- This command is only available on Requests v2.16.4 and greater. titulo: documentation for requests.session.request(verify=...) duplicates requests.request() even where it is different
corpo: [Docs currently state](https://requests.readthedocs.io/en/latest/api/#requests.Session.request):   > Either a boolean, in which case it controls whether we verify the server’s TLS certificate, or a string, in which case it must be a path to a CA bundle to use. Defaults to True.  I suggest rewording both statements, because as they stand they make figuring what went wrong with setting the correct CA bundle way harder than it should be:  1. Passing bool not only controls *whether* the certificate is verified, it [also resets](https://github.com/psf/requests/blob/f43f750ee10addbaa13901c1017631b4d70fd6e3/src/requests/sessions.py#L74) the root store to be verified against. 2. The default for the *method* does **not** behave like True - leaving it unspecified simply defers to the session, as it should.. session in turn may very well have verify=False. 3. (still incomplete because of `os.environ` precedence, but I understand that one is currently #WONTFIX as per https://github.com/psf/requests/issues/3829)  ## Documentation appears to state  |                |s.verify=True | s.verify="/S"|s.verify=False| | -------------- |------------- |------------------- |------------------- | | s.request(verify=True) | True         | ✅ "/S"              | True               | | s.request(verify="/r") | "/r"         | "/r"               | "/r"               | | s.request(verify=False)| False        | False              | False              | | s.request() # i.e. s.request(verify=None) | True         | ⚠️True               | ⚠️True              |  ## Actual Result  |                |s.verify=True | s.verify="/S"|s.verify=False| | -------------- |------------- |------------------- |------------------- | | s.request(verify=True) | True         | ⚠️True               | True               | | s.request(verify="/r") | "/r"         | "/r"               | "/r"               | | s.request(verify=False)| False        | False              | False              | | s.request() # i.e. s.request(verify=None) | True         | ✅"/S"               | ✅ False              |  ## Reproduction Steps  ```python >>> import certifi,requests,ssl,os >>> certifi.__version__ '2026.04.22' >>> certifi.where() '/inaccessible/path' >>> requests.__version__ '2.33.1' >>> session = requests.session() >>> session.verify = ssl.get_default_verify_paths().capath >>> os.path.isdir(session.verify) True >>> session.request(url="https://example.com", method="HEAD") <Response [200]> >>> session.request(url="https://example.com", method="HEAD", verify=True) Traceback (most recent call last): [..]   File "/home/user/lib/python3.10/site-packages/requests/adapters.py", line 304, in cert_verify     raise OSError( OSError: Could not find a suitable TLS CA certificate bundle, invalid path: /inaccessible/path ```  This result means that libraries that opt to use the supposedly-default parameter value of True are doing something meaningfully different from those that use the actual-default parameter of None (typically: by not mentioning the parameter).  ## System Information      $ python -m requests.help  ```json {   "chardet": {     "version": "4.0.0"   },   "charset_normalizer": {     "version": "3.4.4"   },   "cryptography": {     "version": ""   },   "idna": {     "version": "3.3"   },   "implementation": {     "name": "CPython",     "version": "3.10.12"   },   "platform": {     "release": "6.8.0-110-generic",     "system": "Linux"   },   "pyOpenSSL": {     "openssl_version": "",     "version": null   },   "requests": {     "version": "2.33.1"   },   "system_ssl": {     "version": "30000020"   },   "urllib3": {     "version": "2.6.3"   },   "using_charset_normalizer": false,   "using_pyopenssl": false } ```

titulo: Tweak urllib3 version checker
corpo: Hello,  Tiny corner case issue: building urllib3 on my side, I append a marker in the version string to distinguish theses builds, eg.: 2.6.3.build1  Would you consider a small change in requests and split the version string the same way it is done for chardet or charset normalizer ? It would prevent the check from failing on the `major, minor, patch = urllib3_version` line.  ```diff diff --git a/src/requests/__init__.py b/src/requests/__init__.py @@ -56,7 +56,7 @@ except ImportError:      def check_compatibility(urllib3_version, chardet_version, charset_normalizer_version): -    urllib3_version = urllib3_version.split(".") +    urllib3_version = urllib3_version.split(".")[:3]      assert urllib3_version != ["dev"]  # Verify urllib3 isn't installed from git.        # Sometimes, urllib3 only reports its version as 16.1. ```  Regards.

titulo: [Docs] Sidebar is hidden in mobile layout
corpo: ## Problem Description  Theoretically, for documentation using the [alabaster](https://github.com/sphinx-doc/alabaster) theme, the sidebar content should appear at either the **very top** or the **very bottom** in a mobile layout. For example:  - https://alabaster.readthedocs.io/ - https://docs.kernel.org/ - https://www.writethedocs.org/  However, I noticed that the current Requests documentation fails to display sidebar content in its mobile layout.  Based on a preliminary investigation, this issue seems to be caused by modifications to `sphinxsidebar` within the current `custom.css`:  https://github.com/psf/requests/blob/4b0b1a3e9f2fc21b9dcd8b906f2ff02645aa697e/docs/_static/custom.css#L9-L13  The simplest fix is to delete the following line:  ```   div.sphinxsidebar {display: none;} ```

titulo: <spam>
corpo: ## Summary  We ran [HefestoAI](https://github.com/artvepa80/Agents-Hefesto) (deterministic static analysis, no AI/LLM) against Requests (48 files). The codebase is remarkably clean — only one finding in core code worth noting.  ## Finding  ### Session lifecycle — `requests/adapters.py:645`  `urlopen()` return value assigned to `resp` without context manager or explicit `.close()`. Potential connection leak if the response is not fully consumed.  This is a minor finding — urllib3's connection pooling likely handles cleanup. Noted for completeness.  ## What we didn't find  For the most downloaded Python package in history, this is worth saying: Requests is exceptionally well-maintained. Our full scan at severity LOW produced only code style findings (complexity, function length) beyond this single reliability observation. Zero security findings in core code.  ## Reproduction  ```bash pip install hefesto-ai git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/psf/requests.git hefesto analyze requests/ --severity LOW ```  ## About  [HefestoAI](https://github.com/artvepa80/Agents-Hefesto) is an open-source (MIT) deterministic code quality and security analyzer. Sometimes the most useful finding is confirmation that a codebase is clean.

titulo: Localization of The Requests Documentation
corpo: ## Announcement  Hello Requests Community,  I am the author of the @localizethedocs organization. And I’m glad to announce that the 🎉 **requests-docs-l10n** 🎉 project is published now:  - 🚀 **Preview:** [requests-docs-l10n](https://projects.localizethedocs.org/requests-docs-l10n) - 🌐 **Crowdin:** [requests-docs-l10n](https://localizethedocs.crowdin.com/requests-docs-l10n) - 🐙 **GitHub:** [requests-docs-l10n](https://github.com/localizethedocs/requests-docs-l10n)  The goal of this project is to translate The Requests Documentation into multiple languages. Translations are contributed via the Crowdin platform, automatically synchronized with the GitHub repository, and can be previewed on GitHub Pages.  ## How to Contribute Translations?  To contribute the translations to the project, just follow the following steps:  1. Create an account on [Crowdin Enterprise](https://localizethedocs.crowdin.com/u/signup) if you don't have one. 2. Log in and go the [requests-docs-l10n](https://localizethedocs.crowdin.com/requests-docs-l10n) project. 3. Choose the language you would like to contribute.  If translators want to translate a language that is not yet supported, they just need to open a new [issue](https://github.com/localizethedocs/requests-docs-l10n/issues/new?template=language_request.yml) to request the new language. Once the requested language is added, they can begin translating.  ## How to Keep Content Up-to-date?  An FAQ that is sure to come up in the Requests community is: ***How to keep translations up-to-date?***  First and foremost, in my opinion, the focus should be on how to keep the **"Translatable Content (`msgid`)**" up-to-date, rather than the **"Translations (`msgstr`)**". I will focus on the most critical part of the whole infrastructure here.  In short, the [ci-sphinx-update-pot.yml](https://github.com/localizethedocs/requests-docs-l10n/blob/main/.github/workflows/ci-sphinx-update-pot.yml) workflow will be executed weekly to check the upstream project for any required updates to the document content, which in turn triggers the update of the `.pot` files. If an update is needed, a Pull Request (PR) is automatically created to merge into the `l10n` branch. For example:  - https://github.com/localizethedocs/requests-docs-l10n/pull/2 - https://github.com/localizethedocs/requests-docs-l10n/pull/3  Once those PRs are merged, the [ci-gettext-update-po.yml](https://github.com/localizethedocs/requests-docs-l10n/blob/main/.github/workflows/ci-gettext-update-po.yml) workflow will be triggered to merge the updated content from the `.pot` files into the `.po` files for each language. This is essentially how it keeps the "Translatable Content" up-to-date.  Therefore, the core responsibility of the code maintainers, besides ensuring the stable operation of the scripts and workflows, is to regularly _**check whether there are any pending PRs that need to be merged**_.  ## How to Reuse Translations?  If the upstream project or anyone wants to reuse the translated `.po` files prepared by the `requests-docs-l10n` project, they can clone the `.po` files from the `po/${VERSION}` branch by using the following command:  ```bash git clone --depth=1 --branch=po/${VERSION} https://github.com/localizethedocs/requests-docs-l10n.git docs/locale ```  Those `po/${VERSION}` branches are created to facilitate reusage by the upstream project. For instance, the `zh_TW` documentation for the `latest` version can be generated using the commands below:  ```bash BRANCH=main VERSION=latest LANGUAGE=zh_TW BUILDER=html  # Prepare the repository and environment git clone --branch=${BRANCH} https://github.com/psf/requests.git requests-docs cd requests-docs conda create --prefix ./.conda --yes conda activate ./.conda conda install python=3.13 -c conda-forge -c nodefaults --yes export PYTHONNOUSERSITE=1 pip install . -r docs/requirements.txt  # Clone the .po files to the 'locale' directory git clone --branch=po/${VERSION} --depth=1 https://github.com/localizethedocs/requests-docs-l10n.git docs/locale  # Build the documentation sphinx-build \     -b ${BUILDER} \     -D language=${LANGUAGE} \     -D locale_dirs=locale \     -D gettext_compact=0 \     -D gettext_additional_targets=index,literal-block,raw \     docs \     docs/_build/${LANGUAGE}  # Preview the documentation firefox docs/_build/${LANGUAGE}/index.html ```  ## Related Discussions  There were issues and PRs related to documentation translations:  - https://github.com/psf/requests/issues/3033 - https://github.com/psf/requests/issues/624 - https://github.com/psf/requests/issues/5902 - https://github.com/psf/requests/issues/5518 - https://github.com/psf/requests/issues/2750 - https://github.com/psf/requests/issues/5679 - https://github.com/psf/requests/issues/3221 - https://github.com/psf/requests/issues/2744 - https://github.com/psf/requests/issues/6142 - https://github.com/psf/requests/pull/1330 - https://github.com/psf/requests/pull/2746 - https://github.com/psf/requests/pull/2751 - https://github.com/psf/requests/pull/6144  And the @requests community **once** actively maintained documentation translations through the "source translation" method:  - Chinese: https://github.com/requests/requests-docs-cn - Japanese: https://github.com/requests/requests-docs-jp - German: https://github.com/requests/requests-docs-de - French: https://github.com/requests/requests-docs-fr - Polish: https://github.com/requests/requests-docs-pl - Portuguese: https://github.com/requests/requests-docs-pt - Dutch: https://github.com/requests/requests-docs-nl - Bulgarian: https://github.com/requests/requests-docs-bg - Arabic: https://github.com/requests/requests-docs-ar - Danish: https://github.com/requests/requests-docs-da - Italian: https://github.com/requests/requests-docs-it  However, these efforts were eventually abandoned and became unmaintainable for various reasons. Notably, issue #3033 suggested migrating documentation translations to a TMS platform. Therefore, I believe that the `requests-docs-l10n` project should be able to serve this purpose.

titulo: [Docs] No clickable button in other pages can return back to the Home page
corpo: ## Problem Description When visiting the [Quickstart](https://requests.readthedocs.io/en/latest/user/quickstart/) page of the Requests documentation, there is currently no clickable button to return to the [Home](https://requests.readthedocs.io/en/latest/) page. This could be resolved if other pages (including Quickstart) featured a logo at the top of the left sidebar that links back to the home page, consistent with the Home page itself. The cause of this behavior seems to be as follows: First, in the `html_sidebars` configuration within `conf.py`, the top sidebar template is set to `sidebarintro.html` only for the `index` page. For all other pages, the top template is set to `sidebarlogo.html`: https://github.com/psf/requests/blob/ef439eb779c1eba7cbdeeeb302b11e1e061b4b7d/docs/conf.py#L174-L184 Currently, the hyperlinked logo is only implemented in `sidebarintro.html`: https://github.com/psf/requests/blob/ef439eb779c1eba7cbdeeeb302b11e1e061b4b7d/docs/_templates/sidebarintro.html#L1-L5

titulo: `check_header_validity` does not reject null bytes and ASCII control characters in header names and values
corpo:
**Summary:** `check_header_validity` in `requests/utils.py` silently accepts null bytes (`\x00`) and other ASCII control characters (`\x01`–`\x1f`, `\x7f`) in both header names and values. RFC 7230 Section 3.2.6 forbids these characters in header fields. Only `` and `
` are currently caught.   **Expected Result:** `check_header_validity` should raise `InvalidHeader` for any header name or value containing null bytes or ASCII control characters, consistent with how `` and `
` are already handled.   **Actual Result:** ```python from requests.utils import check_header_validity check_header_validity(('X-Test', 'val\x00ue'))   # no error raised check_header_validity(('X-Test', 'val\x01ue'))   # no error raised check_header_validity(('X-Test\x00', 'value'))   # no error raised ```   **Reproduction Steps:** ```python from requests.utils import check_header_validity from requests.exceptions import InvalidHeader  # All of these should raise InvalidHeader but do not: check_header_validity(('X-Test', 'val\x00ue')) check_header_validity(('X-Test', '\x01value')) check_header_validity(('X-Test', 'value\x7f')) check_header_validity(('X-Test\x00', 'value'))  # These correctly raise InvalidHeader: # check_header_validity(('X-Test', 'val
ue'))   # blocked # check_header_validity(('X-Test', 'value'))   # blocked ```   **System Information:** ```bash $ python -m requests.help ```

titulo: Clarify problematic chardet dependency warning
corpo: ## How to reproduce  Install requests and chardet in a clean environment:  ```bash mkdir test && cd test && uv init uv add requests chardet uv run python -c "import requests" ```  At the time of writing (requests=2.32.5, chardet=7.2.0), this gives a warning which is hard to understand, and is not actionable:  > RequestsDependencyWarning: urllib3 (2.6.3) or chardet (7.2.0)/charset_normalizer (3.4.6) doesn't match a supported version!   ## Explanation  I spent around 15 minutes trying to get rid of this warning, thinking that maybe my network requests would somehow be broken. I tried to install different versions of urllib3, chardet and charset-normalizer. After reading issues and docs, I found the full explanation to be: requests uses `chardet` only if it's installed (optional dependency). Otherwise it uses `charset-normalizer`. I think this behavior is questionable - consider that I didn't even install chardet myself, one of my other dependencies had chardet as its dependency. Why would that alter the behavior of requests?  Furthermore, I had to go into requests code to understand what chardet version was actually supported, which is not a very good developer experience.  ## Suggestion  If existing behavior is kept, I suggest to at least reword the warning, e.g.: > The requests library uses chardet as an optional dependency. You have chardet==7.2.0, but requests supports chardet<6. Please install chardet<6 to silence this warning.

titulo: RFC: Adding inline type annotations to Requests
corpo: > [!IMPORTANT] > **Before reporting new issues,** be sure to check [this comment](https://github.com/psf/requests/issues/7271#issuecomment-4424268705) to see if your problem is already being addressed.  ## Motivation  Requests has notably been without inline type annotations since type hints entered the Python ecosystem. We've had aspirations of bringing Requests up to par with community standards for a few years but have been unable to properly express the typing contract. This change doesn't solve all of those gaps, but does make progress towards that goal.  The maintainers of typeshed have provided an incredibly useful alternative for Requests typing for quite a while. There are some limitations of type stubs that can't fully express the Requests API though. Cases like `iter_content` having different return typing based on input, or PreparedRequests needing to be state checked can't be easily expressed. Inline annotations let us own the type contract alongside the code and should help drive better development decisions in the future.  For most use cases, the public API should be accurately typed. There are some internals that are currently suppressed because they need discussion, but the package passes pyright strict mode without errors. We've flagged where the sharp edges are and can refine those over time.  The main goal is to start this migration with community input to make sure we're covering all usage. The "magic" of Requests is that it's very flexible, which also means people use it in creative ways the maintainers don't always anticipate. We want to identify those edge cases early in this process before the types ship in a release.  ## What's changed  - Every class, function, method, and module-level variable in `src/requests/` is annotated - No public API changes - Passes typechecking with pyright strict mode - New internal `_types.py` module for shared type aliases and Protocols - `from __future__ import annotations` applied everywhere - There are some minor bug fixes included, but they address legitimate defects in Requests that resulted in unhandled runtime exceptions.  ## Design philosophy  **Types should describe the code, not change behavior.** This was the primary goal in this process, not adding new constraints.  Where typing forced a choice between runtime strictness and backward compatibility, we chose backward compatibility. That's the lens I'd view this through when things may differ from expectations.  ## How to test  Install from the branch:  ``` python -m pip install git+https://github.com/psf/requests.git@inline_types_rfc ```  or  ``` uv pip install git+https://github.com/psf/requests.git@inline_types_rfc ```  Then:  - Run your existing test suite - Run pyright or mypy against your code that uses Requests - Try your usual Requests patterns and see if anything doesn't typecheck  ## What feedback we're looking for  > [!IMPORTANT] > We want feedback from people who actively maintain projects that depend on Requests or use it heavily. Please share your real experience testing this against your code. > > Comments that are clearly AI-generated will be hidden or removed. This is a library written "for Humans". The conversation is between maintainers and users, not a prompt.  If you do find issues, we want to hear about it. Specifically:  - **Compatibility**: Does this break anything in your project? Especially if you're doing something unusual with Requests internals. - **Type accuracy**: Do the types match how you actually use the API? Are return types too narrow or too wide? - **Missing coverage**: Is there a pattern you use that we're not covering?  We're not looking for style opinions on the annotations themselves or nitpicks on suppression comments. Those are tracked on the PR.  ## Known limitations  - **`str | bytes` URL handling**: Requests has historically accepted both `str` and `bytes` for URLs. The typing currently declares `str` only. This is a known gap we're still working through. - **urllib3 stub gaps**: Some `type: ignore` comments exist because urllib3's type stubs don't fully cover all the methods we use. - **Optional dependency typing**: chardet/charset_normalizer detection is imperfect under strict mode since these are optional imports. - **`RequestsCookieJar` and `MutableMapping`**: The RequestsCookieJar's conformance to `MutableMapping` has some known mismatches (extended method signatures, `__iter__` yielding `Cookie` objects instead of strings) that date back to when the class was first written against the Python 2.6 ABC contract. The current types don't fix that, but should be clearer about what the class does. Future work may be able to refine this further.  For more details and rationale, see the [PR](https://github.com/psf/requests/pull/7272).

titulo: Follow redirects - timeout waiting for connection to close
corpo: <!-- Summary. --> When requests sees a redirect header, it waits until the connection has closed before following it. This can cause timeout errors.  ## Expected Result  The redirect should be followed immediately. <!-- What you expected. -->  ## Actual Result Requests waits for the body before following, which may cause it to timeout. <!-- What happened instead. -->  ## Reproduction Steps Consider this server: ```php <?php header( "Location: https://example.com/" ); //   Long operation. sleep(10); die(); ```  That immediately sends:  ``` < HTTP/2 302  < location: https://example.com/ ```  But then waits before closing the connection.  A simple Python request:  ```python import requests requests.get("https://example.com/test.php", stream=True, allow_redirects=True) ```  Waits for 10 seconds before following the redirect. titulo: New chardet version
corpo: I apologise in advance for what may be a complete non-issue. I do not have the skills or the time to comb through the chardet codebase for potential backdoors.  The chardet project has recently released a new version(7) that was "rewritten from the ground up". Although most of the buzz around this is about the license changing from LGPL to MIT, I am concerned that a trusted component of practically every python internet-connected application has been swapped out for a completely new codebase. And it seems requests has accepted this by bumping the chardet version requirement to < 8.0.  If someone wanted to compromise every python app in the world, backdooring chardet would seem to be a great solution, given it processes every piece of user data. Making an incremental change to do this would risk easy discovery, so claiming a complete rewrite makes verification a massively harder (and therefore more unlikely) job.  I really hope someone smarter than me can explain why this could not happen. Otherwise it would seem prudent to move the chardet version requirement back to < 7.0 until chardet has been reliably vetted.

titulo: MockResponse.getheaders() has two bugs: missing return and nonexistent method call
corpo:
## Summary
 
 `MockResponse.getheaders(name)` in `src/requests/cookies.py` has been silently broken since it was introduced. There are two distinct bugs in the same line:
 
 ```python
 def getheaders(self, name):
     self._headers.getheaders(name)   # line 121
 ```
 
 1. **Missing `return` statement** -- the result is discarded; `None` is always returned to every caller.
 2. **Nonexistent method** -- `self._headers` is an `http.client.HTTPMessage` instance (which inherits from `email.message.Message`). `HTTPMessage` has no `getheaders()` method. Any real call to `MockResponse.getheaders()` raises `AttributeError`.
 
 ## Why it went unnoticed
 
 `MockResponse.getheaders()` is dead code in practice. Tracing the call path:
 
 - `extract_cookies_to_jar()` creates a `MockResponse` and passes it to `jar.extract_cookies(res, req)`.
 - Python's `http.cookiejar.CookieJar.extract_cookies()` calls `response.info()` to retrieve the `HTTPMessage`, then calls `headers.get_all("Set-Cookie", [])` and `headers.get_all("Set-Cookie2", [])` directly on the returned object.
 - The cookiejar never calls `response.getheaders()`.
 
 This explains why neither bug has had any observable production impact.
 
 ## Proposed options
 
 I wanted to raise this here before submitting a patch, since the right outcome is not obvious:
 
 1. **Fix it** -- replace the body with `return self._headers.get_all(name, [])`. `get_all(name, failobj)` is the correct `email.message.Message` API for retrieving all values of a header by name in Python 3. This keeps the interface intact in case any third-party code (e.g. custom adapters) is calling `getheaders()` on a `MockResponse`-like object.
 
 2. **Remove it** -- delete `getheaders()` entirely. The method is not called anywhere in the library and was never functional, so removing it would eliminate a misleading public interface without any regression risk.
 
 3. **Leave as-is** -- if the view is that the method is harmless dead code not worth touching, I am happy to drop this.
 
 Happy to submit a PR for whichever option you prefer. I will wait for direction before opening anything.

titulo: RequestsCookieJar shouldn't inherit from MutableMapping
corpo: <!-- Summary. -->  `RequestsCookieJar` currently inherits from both `CookieJar` and `MutableMapping`, but these classes are incompatible. `CookieJar.__iter__` iterates over `Cookies`, whereas `MutableMapping` expects `__iter__` to iterate over the key type (`str`).  ## Expected Result  `RequestsCookieJar` does not inherit from `MutableMapping`  (or the values produced by `__iter__` can be passed to `__getitem__`)  ## Actual Result  `__iter__` produces `Cookie`s, and `__getitem__` raises `KeyError` if any non-`str` is passed  ## Reproduction Steps  ```python from collections.abc import MutableMapping import requests  # this function should work with any object that correctly implements MutableMapping def example(some_obj):     print(f"example(some_obj:{type(some_obj).__name__})")     if isinstance(some_obj, MutableMapping):         for key in some_obj:             print(f"some_obj[{key!r}] = {some_obj[key]!r}")  example("") example({"foo": 1})  cookie_jar = requests.cookies.RequestsCookieJar() cookie_jar["foo"] = "1" example(cookie_jar) # raises KeyError ```  ## System Information      $ python -m requests.help  ```json {   "chardet": {     "version": null   },   "charset_normalizer": {     "version": "3.4.3"   },   "cryptography": {     "version": ""   },   "idna": {     "version": "3.11"   },   "implementation": {     "name": "CPython",     "version": "3.13.11"   },   "platform": {     "release": "6.12.70",     "system": "Linux"   },   "pyOpenSSL": {     "openssl_version": "",     "version": null   },   "requests": {     "version": "2.32.5"   },   "system_ssl": {     "version": "30600010"   },   "urllib3": {     "version": "2.5.0"   },   "using_charset_normalizer": true,   "using_pyopenssl": false } ```  but this should apply to any version since 4d6871d9176c13affe625b1885278d396a39f21d  ## Additional context  This is particularly a problem for correctly typing `RequestsCookieJar`, which is how I ran into this. See https://github.com/python/typeshed/issues/15457

titulo: Chardet is used, when it is available, not when `[use-chardet-on-py3]`-extra is installed
corpo: First: IMHO this is related to but not a duplicate of #5871 #7222 #7219  `requests` tries to use `chardet` when it can be imported. However, IMHO it should only use it, if `requests` was installed with the `[use-chardet-on-py3]`-extra.  As reported in #7219, `requests` shows a warning, when the version of `chardet` does not fulfill the requirements. However, package managers like `uv` won't respect the version requirement of the dependency of `requests` on `chardet`, when the extra is not installed (see https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/issues/18179). If another project dependency depends on `chardet`, it will be installed, but the version of `chardet` might not fulfill the requirement of `requests`. titulo: TooManyRedirects exception loop when requesting FQDN URLs with a trailing dot
corpo: **Describe the bug** When making a request to a URL with a Fully Qualified Domain Name (FQDN) that includes a trailing dot (e.g., `https://pyropus.ca./`), `requests` gets stuck in an infinite redirect loop, eventually raising a `requests.exceptions.TooManyRedirects` exception.   This happens because the server attempts to redirect the user to the non-FQDN version (without the dot), but `requests` seems to mishandle the Host header or the redirect state with the trailing dot, causing it to loop infinitely.  **To Reproduce** ```python import requests  res = requests.get("https://pyropus.ca./")  ```  **Expected behavior** The request should successfully follow the redirect to the non-FQDN URL (`https://pyropus.ca/`) and return a `200 OK` status code, just like web browsers (Chrome/Firefox) or `curl` do.  **Workaround found** If we manually inject the Host header without the trailing dot, it bypasses the loop and returns `200`: ```python custom_headers = {'Host': 'pyropus.ca'} res = requests.get("https://pyropus.ca./", headers=custom_headers) print(res.status_code) ```  **System Information** - `requests` version: Latest - Python version: 3.10+ - OS: Linux  **Context** This was discovered while debugging a redirect loop issue inside the Fedora Infrastructure (Anitya project).

titulo: AttributeError when passing None to utility functions (get_encoding_from_headers, parse_header_links)
corpo: ## Summary  Several utility functions in `requests.utils` crash with `AttributeError` when passed `None` instead of returning a sensible default or raising a clear `TypeError`. This can cause unexpected crashes in application code that doesn't defensively check for `None` before calling these functions.  ## Affected Functions  ### 1. `get_encoding_from_headers(None)`  ```python >>> from requests.utils import get_encoding_from_headers >>> get_encoding_from_headers(None) AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'get' ```  ### 2. `parse_header_links(None)`  ```python >>> from requests.utils import parse_header_links >>> parse_header_links(None) AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'strip' ```  ## Expected Behavior  These functions should either: 1. Return a sensible default (`None` or `[]`) when passed `None`, OR 2. Raise a clear `TypeError` with a helpful message  ## Actual Behavior  Both functions raise confusing `AttributeError` exceptions that don't clearly indicate the problem is with the input.  ## Reproduction Steps  ```python import requests print(f"requests version: {requests.__version__}")  from requests.utils import get_encoding_from_headers, parse_header_links  # Test 1 try:     get_encoding_from_headers(None) except AttributeError as e:     print(f"get_encoding_from_headers(None) -> AttributeError: {e}")  # Test 2 try:     parse_header_links(None) except AttributeError as e:     print(f"parse_header_links(None) -> AttributeError: {e}") ```  ## Real-World Scenario  A developer might reasonably write code like this:  ```python # Get Link header (returns None if not present) link_header = response.headers.get('Link')  # Parse it - crashes if header wasn't present! links = parse_header_links(link_header) ```  This pattern is common and the crash is unexpected.  ## System Information  ``` $ python -m requests.help # requests 2.32.5 # Python 3.13 # macOS ```  ## Suggested Fix  Add input validation at the start of each function:  ```python def get_encoding_from_headers(headers):     if headers is None:         return None     # ... rest of function  def parse_header_links(value):     if not value:         return []     # ... rest of function ```  Note: `parse_header_links` already handles empty string (returns `[]`), so handling `None` the same way would be consistent.

titulo: PERF: `df.loc[row, cols]` returns a small Series that keeps a `(len(cols), len(df))` temporary array alive (regression from 2.x)
corpo: ### Pandas version checks  - [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported. - [x] I have confirmed this issue exists on the latest version of pandas. - [x] I have confirmed this issue exists on the main branch of pandas.  ### Reproducible Example  ```python import tracemalloc  import numpy as np import pandas as pd  n = 100_000 df = pd.DataFrame({c: np.zeros(n) for c in "abcd"})  res = df.loc[0, ["a", "b", "d"]] print(getattr(res.values.base, "shape", None))  # (3, 100000)  tracemalloc.start() results = [df.loc[0, ["a", "b", "d"]] for _ in range(100)] print(f"{tracemalloc.get_traced_memory()[0] / 2**20:.0f} MiB")  # 100 Series of 3 floats ```  Output on 3.0.6 and on main (`3.1.0.dev0+2036.gbe9eebf87e`):  ``` (3, 100000) 229 MiB ```  Selecting one row and a non-contiguous list of columns returns a 3-element Series. That Series is a view into a `(3, n)` array, which is a temporary copy made by the column selection, not the DataFrame's own storage. Each result keeps about 2.3 MB alive for 24 bytes of data, and the cost grows with `len(df)`. Collecting lookups like this in a loop leads to large memory growth.  `df.iloc[0, [0, 1, 3]]` and `df[cols].loc[0]` behave the same way. Selecting the row first (`df.loc[0][cols]`) does not.  ### Installed Versions  <details>  ```  INSTALLED VERSIONS ------------------ commit                : 2905718b126579d2cf0fe5bae05bd75facb67d77 python                : 3.14.3 python-bits           : 64 OS                    : Darwin OS-release            : 25.4.0 Version               : Darwin Kernel Version 25.4.0: Thu Mar 19 19:33:43 PDT 2026; root:xnu-12377.101.15~1/RELEASE_ARM64_T8142 machine               : arm64 processor             : arm byteorder             : little LC_ALL                : None LANG                  : en_US.UTF-8 LOCALE                : en_US.UTF-8  pandas                : 3.0.6 numpy                 : 2.5.3 dateutil              : 2.9.0.post0 pip                   : None Cython                : None sphinx                : None IPython               : None adbc-driver-postgresql: None adbc-driver-sqlite    : None bs4                   : None bottleneck            : None fastparquet           : None fsspec                : None html5lib              : None hypothesis            : None gcsfs                 : None jinja2                : None lxml.etree            : None matplotlib            : None numba                 : None numexpr               : None odfpy                 : None openpyxl              : None psycopg2              : None pymysql               : None pyarrow               : None pyiceberg             : None pyreadstat            : None pytest                : None python-calamine       : None pytz                  : None pyxlsb                : None s3fs                  : None scipy                 : None sqlalchemy            : None tables                : None tabulate              : None xarray                : None xlrd                  : None xlsxwriter            : None zstandard             : None qtpy                  : None pyqt5                 : None ```  </details>  ### Prior Performance  On pandas 2.3.3 the same example prints:  ``` None 0 MiB ```  The result owns its data, and there is no memory growth. With `mode.copy_on_write = True`, 2.3.3 prints `(3,)` and `0 MiB`, so the result is still backed only by its 3 values. The behavior is present from 3.0.0 through 3.0.6 and on main.

titulo: BUG: `Day` offset stub base skips `SingleConstructorOffset`
corpo: - [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported. - [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas. - [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.  ### Reproducible Example  ```python from pandas._libs.tslibs.offsets import Day print(Day.__bases__) ```  ### Issue Description  At runtime `Day.__bases__ == (SingleConstructorOffset,)`, but the type stub `pandas/_libs/tslibs/offsets.pyi:130` declares `class Day(BaseOffset)`, skipping `SingleConstructorOffset`. The Cython source `pandas/_libs/tslibs/offsets.pyx:1517` has `cdef class Day(SingleConstructorOffset)`, and `Day` is the only offset whose stub base skips `SingleConstructorOffset` (every other offset reaches it through its declared base).  ### Expected Behavior  `offsets.pyi` should declare `class Day(SingleConstructorOffset): ...` so the stub matches the Cython source and the runtime `__bases__`.  ### Installed Versions  This is a stub/source inconsistency rather than a version-dependent behavior; it is present on the `main` branch (offsets.pyx / offsets.pyi as of be9eebf87e).

titulo: BUG: .str and .dt accessors raise on dictionary-encoded ArrowDtype
corpo: On current main, the `.str` and `.dt` accessors reject Series backed by dictionary-encoded `ArrowDtype`, even though the equivalent plain `ArrowDtype` (and `Categorical`, for `.str`) work fine.  Repro:  ```python import pandas as pd import pyarrow as pa import datetime  # .str on dictionary-encoded strings s = pd.Series(     pd.array(['a', 'b', 'a'],              dtype=pd.ArrowDtype(pa.dictionary(pa.int32(), pa.string()))) ) s.str.upper() # AttributeError: Can only use .str accessor with string values, not unknown-array  # .dt on dictionary-encoded timestamps arr = pa.DictionaryArray.from_arrays(     pa.array([0, 1, 0], type=pa.int32()),     pa.array([datetime.datetime(2020, 1, 1), datetime.datetime(2020, 1, 2)],              type=pa.timestamp('us')), ) s2 = pd.Series(pd.arrays.ArrowExtensionArray(arr)) s2.dt.year # AttributeError: Can only use .dt accessor with datetimelike values ```  Expected: both accessors work, decoding through the dictionary the way `Categorical` does (`pd.Series(pd.Categorical(['a', 'b', 'a'])).str.upper()` works fine).  What I found reading the code:  - `.str`: `StringMethods._validate` does `values = getattr(data, "categories", data)` to blow up categoricals before inferring. `ArrowExtensionArray` has no `.categories`, so `lib.infer_dtype` sees the raw arrow array and returns `"unknown-array"`, which is not in the allowed list. - `.dt`: `CombinedDatetimelikeProperties.__init__` gates the arrow path on `data.dtype.kind in "Mm"`. `ArrowDtype.kind` only returns `"M"` when `pa.types.is_timestamp(self.pyarrow_dtype)` is true, which is false for dictionary types, so it falls back to the numpy object kind `"O"`.  So both accessors need to look through dictionary encoding to the value type, similar to how categoricals are handled.  Environment: pandas main (3.2.0.dev1), pyarrow 25.0.1, Python 3.12, Linux.

titulo: BUG: to_json(date_format="iso") segfaults on a failed allocation — NpyDateTimeToIsoCallback returns NULL without setting errorMsg
corpo: ### Pandas version checks  - [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported. - [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the latest version of pandas. - [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the main branch of pandas.  ### Reproducible Example  `int64ToIso` returns `NULL` only when its allocation fails, so the example injects a single failed `malloc` of the exact size it requests (42 bytes for `date_unit="ms"`) with an `LD_PRELOAD` shim. Nothing else about the frame is unusual.  ```c // failmalloc.c — gcc -shared -fPIC -o failmalloc.so failmalloc.c -ldl #define _GNU_SOURCE #include <dlfcn.h> #include <stddef.h> #include <stdio.h>  static size_t target_size = 0; static int armed = 0, fired = 0;  void failmalloc_arm(size_t size) { target_size = size; armed = 1; fired = 0; }  void *malloc(size_t size) {   static void *(*real)(size_t) = NULL;   if (!real)     real = dlsym(RTLD_NEXT, "malloc");   if (armed && !fired && size == target_size) {     fired = 1;     fprintf(stderr, "[failmalloc] returning NULL for size=%zu\n", size);     return NULL;   }   return real(size); } ```  ```python # repro.py import ctypes, faulthandler import pandas as pd  faulthandler.enable()  frame = pd.DataFrame({"t": pd.to_datetime([1616409000123] * 50, unit="ms").as_unit("ms")})  ctypes.CDLL("./failmalloc.so").failmalloc_arm(ctypes.c_size_t(42))  print(frame.to_json(orient="records", date_format="iso")) ```  ``` $ PYTHONMALLOC=malloc LD_PRELOAD=./failmalloc.so python repro.py [failmalloc] returning NULL for size=42 Fatal Python error: Segmentation fault  Current thread 0x0000004002102f00 [python] (most recent call first):   File ".../pandas/io/json/_json.py", line 292 in write   File ".../pandas/io/json/_json.py", line 241 in to_json   File ".../pandas/core/generic.py", line 2623 in to_json   File "repro.py", line 12 in <module>  Current thread's C stack trace (most recent call first):   ...   Binary file ".../pandas/_libs/json.cpython-314-x86_64-linux-gnu.so", at +0x8ae0 ```  ### Issue Description  A failed allocation inside the ISO datetime conversion is dereferenced as a `NULL` string instead of raising, because the encoder's `NULL` signal is `enc->errorMsg` and this path never sets it:  1. `int64ToIso` (`pandas/_libs/src/datetime/date_conversions.c`) allocates the output buffer and    returns `NULL` after `PyErr_NoMemory()` if that fails. It also returns `NULL` when    `make_iso_8601_datetime` fails. 2. `NpyDateTimeToIsoCallback` (`pandas/_libs/src/vendored/ujson/python/objToJSON.c`) forwards    that result unchanged, without setting `((JSONObjectEncoder *)tc->encoder)->errorMsg`. 3. `ultrajsonenc.c`, `case JT_UTF8`, tests only `enc->errorMsg` before using the value:  ```c     value = enc->getStringValue(obj, &tc, &szlen);     if (enc->errorMsg) {       enc->endTypeContext(obj, &tc);       return;     }     Buffer_Reserve(enc, RESERVE_STRING(szlen));     ...       if (!Buffer_EscapeStringUnvalidated(enc, value, value + szlen)) { ```  So `Buffer_EscapeStringUnvalidated` runs on `value == NULL`, which segfaults.  Sibling callbacks in the same file follow the opposite convention and do set `errorMsg` before returning `NULL` — `PyTimeToJSON` and the type-check branch of `PyDateTimeToIsoCallback` both do `((JSONObjectEncoder *)tc->encoder)->errorMsg = "";`. Two more callbacks look to have the same gap as the one above:  - `NpyTimeDeltaToIsoCallback` forwards `int64ToIsoDuration`, which has the same two `NULL`   returns. - `PyDateTimeToIsoCallback` sets `errorMsg` for the type check, but forwards the result of   `PyDateTimeToIso` (which has several `NULL` returns) unchecked.  This looks like a remaining instance of the class of bug reported in #66356 and fixed by #66357 and #66797 — neither of those passes touched the ISO datetime/timedelta callbacks.  Reproduced on 3.0.5 and on `main` at `3.1.0.dev0+2036.gbe9eebf87e`, both Python 3.14 / linux-x86_64. 3.0.6 contains no changes to these files.  For context on why this isn't only theoretical: we hit a SIGSEGV in `pandas/_libs/json...so` beneath `DataFrame.to_json(orient="records", date_format="iso")` in CI, serialising a ~45k-row frame with a tz-aware `datetime64[ms, UTC]` column under memory pressure from several parallel test workers. I can't attribute that crash with certainty — the shipped extension module is stripped, so the C stack has no symbols — but this is the only unchecked-`NULL` path I could find on it, and the per-value allocation count makes a transient failure plausible.  ### Expected Behavior  `MemoryError` (or the relevant exception) propagates to the caller, consistent with how other allocation failures in the encoder are handled — e.g. `Buffer_Realloc` calls `SetError(NULL, enc, "Could not reserve memory block")`.  Setting `errorMsg` in the three callbacks before returning `NULL` would be enough; adding a `value == NULL` check alongside the `enc->errorMsg` check in `JT_UTF8` would make the encoder robust to any future callback with the same omission.  ### Installed Versions  <details>  ``` INSTALLED VERSIONS ------------------ commit                : e68db09ecf6427d1b62e565bacf17f2e525a3032 python                : 3.14.7 python-bits           : 64 OS                    : Linux machine               : x86_64 byteorder             : little LOCALE                : C.UTF-8  pandas                : 3.0.5 numpy                 : 2.5.3 ```  Also reproduced on `3.1.0.dev0+2036.gbe9eebf87e` (nightly wheel).  </details>

titulo: ENH: Add optional checkpointing and recovery for long-running apply operations
corpo: ### Feature Type  - [x] Adding new functionality to pandas  - [x] Changing existing functionality in pandas  - [ ] Removing existing functionality in pandas   ### Problem Description  Long-running Series.apply() and DataFrame.apply() operations can be vulnerable to unexpected process or kernel termination.  Currently, intermediate results are kept in memory until the operation completes. If the Python process terminates unexpectedly, all successfully computed intermediate results may be lost, even if most or all rows have already been processed.  It would be useful to provide an optional checkpointing mechanism that periodically persists completed results during apply() execution.  For example, users could specify a checkpoint file and checkpoint interval. If execution is interrupted, a subsequent run could restore the checkpoint and continue processing only the remaining rows.  This could be particularly useful for expensive per-row operations such as API requests, machine learning inference, LLM calls, network operations, or computationally expensive transformations.  The goal would not be to handle the process crash itself, since pandas cannot execute recovery code after the process has already terminated. Instead, intermediate results would be persisted proactively during normal execution so that they can be recovered afterwards.  ### Feature Description  result = df[“column”].apply( expensive_function, checkpoint=“apply_checkpoint.pkl”, checkpoint_every=10, )  ### Alternative Solutions  for i, value in df["column"].items():     df.at[i, "result"] = expensive_function(value)      if i % 10 == 0:         df.to_pickle("checkpoint.pkl")  ### Additional Context  _No response_

titulo: BUG: loc assignment of a length-1 NumPy array into a PyArrow column raises TypeError
corpo: ### Pandas version checks  - [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.  - [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.  - [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.   ### Reproducible Example  ```python import pandas as pd  df = pd.DataFrame({"A": pd.array([5000.0], dtype="double[pyarrow]")}) df.loc[:, "A"] = df["A"].astype(float).round(6) # TypeError: Invalid value '[5000.]' for dtype 'double[pyarrow]'  df2 = pd.DataFrame({"A": pd.array([5000.0, 5000.0], dtype="double[pyarrow]")}) df2.loc[:, "A"] = df2["A"].astype(float).round(6)  # OK ```  ### Issue Description  On a 1-row DataFrame, df.loc[:, col] = <NumPy ndarray/Series> into an existing PyArrow-backed column raises TypeError, even when every value is a valid float (e.g. 5000.0). The same assignment succeeds when the frame has 2 or more rows.  5000.0 is not invalid. The error text is misleading.  What happens:  The RHS is a length-1 float64 array, array([5000.]). SingleBlockManager.setitem_inplace unwraps any 1-d length-1 ndarray to a 0-d array to avoid the NumPy 1.25 deprecation (value[0, ...], added in [#52906](https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/pull/52906)): if isinstance(value, np.ndarray) and value.ndim == 1 and len(value) == 1:     value = value[0, ...]  # array([5000.]) -> array(5000.) is_list_like(array(5000.)) is False, so ArrowExtensionArray._box_pa takes the scalar path. pa.scalar(np.ndarray(...), type=pa.float64()) fails: ArrowInvalid: Could not convert array(5000.) with type numpy.ndarray: tried to convert to double pandas 3 rewraps that as TypeError: Invalid value '[5000.]' for dtype 'double[pyarrow]' and, unlike 2.x, does not fall back to recasting the column. This is the same unwrap that #59249 / #57923 / #65452 discuss for object-dtype cells. Here the symptom is different and is a hard error on valid numeric data, not an API question about whether a cell should store array([1.]) vs 1.0.  Related, but not the same report:  https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/issues/59249 https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/issues/57923 https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/issues/65452  ### Expected Behavior  A valid float should be written into the double[pyarrow] column. 1-row and N-row frames should behave the same.  A narrow fix would be enough and does not require settling the whole single-element listlike-RHS matrix in #65452, for example:  in _box_pa_scalar, if value is a 0-d ndarray, use value.item() before pa.scalar, or in setitem_inplace, skip the length-1 unwrap when the target is an ExtensionArray.  ### Installed Versions  <details>  python   : 3.13.5 pandas   : 3.0.5   (also reproduced the failure mode on 3.0.6 source; main still has the unwrap) pyarrow  : 25.0.0 numpy    : 2.5.2 OS       : Windows  On pandas 2.2.3 / 2.3.3 the same assignment does not raise. It emits  FutureWarning: Setting an item of incompatible dtype is deprecated...  and recasts the column to NumPy float64. pandas 3 turned that warning into this TypeError, so the 1-row unwrap now surfaces as a hard failure on Arrow columns.  Confirmed on all released pandas 3.0.x; 3.0.6 fixed a different loc[:, col] Arrow issue (GH 67990, CoW aliasing), not this one.  </details>

titulo: ENH: ArrowExtensionArray should be supported by HDFStore
corpo: ### Feature Type  - [x] Adding new functionality to pandas  - [ ] Changing existing functionality in pandas  - [ ] Removing existing functionality in pandas   ### Problem Description  Currently, writing data containing ArrowExtensionArrays to HDF5 fails. Since Numpy objects are pickled anyways, I don't see why Pandas should not also automatically pickle ArrowExtensionArrays.  For NumPy pickling, see these lines: https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/4fde542d9691acc218c6293165619dcb397e6a8b/pandas/io/pytables.py#L3998-L4001  For a minimal working example (not working) - to test with both pa.array examples:  ``` import pandas as pd import pyarrow as pa  # Nested Arrow array #arr = pa.array([[1, 2], [3], [4, 5, 6]]) arr = pa.array([["123"]])  # DataFrame with Arrow-backed column df = pd.DataFrame(     {         "jets": pd.Series(arr, dtype=pd.ArrowDtype(arr.type))     } )  # Triggers PyTables serialization df.to_hdf("test.h5", key="df") ```  ### Feature Description  The cheapest solution is to add  ```python3             elif isinstance(value.dtype, ArrowDtype):                 vlarr = self._handle.create_vlarray(                     self.group, key, _tables().ObjectAtom(), filters=self._filters                 )                 vlarr.append(value) ```  below the branch https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/4fde542d9691acc218c6293165619dcb397e6a8b/pandas/io/pytables.py#L4024 .  ### Alternative Solutions  One could also check array types and e.g. string arrays could be saved correctly. However then after loading, they are no longer PyArrow data and this does not solve saving arbitrary data.  ### Additional Context  Since Uproot uses ExtensionArrays in https://github.com/scikit-hep/uproot5/pull/734 , Uproot loaded data can no longer always be stored as HDF5. This is described in https://github.com/scikit-hep/uproot5/issues/1706 . It is realistic that Uproot moves to ArrowExtensionArrays - at least I suggested that in Pull Request https://github.com/scikit-hep/uproot5/pull/1718 . Currently it uses `AwkwardExtensionArray` from `awkward-pandas`, but that is deprecated. Meaning the effort of not fearing failures when saving data read from a ROOT file as HDF5 now transferred to making Pandas support `ArrowExtensionArray`s for HDF5 export.
