titulo: API: should the _supports_2d contract require repeat(axis=...)?
corpo: `ExtensionDtype._supports_2d` documents what a third-party array must provide to declare itself 2-D capable (`pandas/core/dtypes/base.py`):  > Arrays that support 2D values should: > > - implement Array.reshape > - subclass the Dim2CompatTests in tests.extension.base > - `_concat_same_type` should support `axis` keyword > - `_reduce` and reductions should support `axis` keyword  `repeat` is not on that list, and the base implementation actively rejects an axis:  ```python # pandas/core/arrays/base.py def repeat(self, repeats, axis: AxisInt | None = None) -> Self:     nv.validate_repeat((), {"axis": axis}) ```  while the backing-array implementation both defaults to and honours one:  ```python # pandas/_libs/arrays.pyx def repeat(self, repeats, axis: int | np.integer = 0): ```  In-tree this never shows, because the only dtypes with `_supports_2d = True` are `DatetimeTZDtype` and `PeriodDtype`, whose arrays are `NDArrayBacked`. A third-party array that implements the four documented requirements and inherits `ExtensionArray.repeat` would raise `ValueError: the 'axis' parameter is not supported in the pandas implementation of repeat()`.  This matters because the gate internals use to decide "may I treat this as 2-D" is  ```python def is_1d_only_ea_dtype(dtype) -> bool:     return isinstance(dtype, ExtensionDtype) and not dtype._supports_2d ```  so anything reaching a 2-D code path is exactly the `_supports_2d` audience. Broadcasting a 1-D value across several columns wants `value.reshape(1, -1).repeat(ncols, axis=0)`, which works for both in-tree types and for any `NDArrayBacked` array, but is not something the documented contract entitles pandas to call.  Two ways to resolve it:  1. Add `repeat` with `axis` support to the `_supports_2d` requirements, and relax the base    signature/validation for 2-D-capable arrays. This documents what pandas already needs and    costs existing third-party authors nothing until they opt into `_supports_2d`. 2. Treat `repeat(axis=)` as out of contract and require internals to spell 2-D broadcasting    with only the four documented operations, e.g. `value.repeat(ncols).reshape(-1, ncols)`.    That is contract-clean but produces a C-contiguous result where the current spelling gives    an F-contiguous one, which changes the stored block's layout on the NumPy path.  No in-tree caller passes `axis=` to an ExtensionArray's `repeat` today, so nothing is broken right now; this is about whether such a call is legitimate going forward.

titulo: BUG: Value-dependent formatting when casting from datetime to string
corpo: ### Pandas version checks  - [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.  - [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.  - [ ] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.   ### Reproducible Example  ```python import pandas as pd import numpy as np  assert pd.__version__ == "3.0.5" assert np.__version__ == "2.5.1"  np.testing.assert_array_equal(     ["1970-01-01 00:00:00.001"],     pd.Series([1], dtype="datetime64[ms]").astype(str),     strict=False ) np.testing.assert_array_equal(     ["1970-01-01 00:00:01"],  # <- value dependent format     pd.Series([1000], dtype="datetime64[ms]").astype(str),     strict=False )  np.testing.assert_array_equal(     ["1970-01-01T00:00:00.001"],     pd.Series([1], dtype="datetime64[ms]").to_numpy().astype(str),     strict=False ) np.testing.assert_array_equal(     ["1970-01-01T00:00:01.000"],  # <- unit dependent format     pd.Series([1000], dtype="datetime64[ms]").to_numpy().astype(str),     strict=False ) ```  ### Issue Description  The string formatting of datetimes depends on the values rather than the time unit of the data type. The analogous operation in NumPy only depends on the unit.  I was not able to find a definitive answer on the matter that clarified whether this is intended behavior. I can see that this may have been intended in pandas 1.x where the one and only unit was `ns` which would lead to very long strings in all cases, despite most users probably never working on a ns resolution.   ### Expected Behavior  My understanding is that value-dependent semantics are not desired in pandas these days(?). Given that pandas allows users to define their desired units these days, it seems reasonable to me to make the formatting depend only on the unit rather than the values. titulo: BUG/DEPR: low_memory keyword in read_csv
corpo:
`low_memory=True` (the default) can give incorrect results in corner cases, which is the reason why the keyword exists.  Minimal example:  ``` N = 65536  # rows in the first internal chunk of an 8-column table data = (     "a,b,c,d,e,f,g,h
"     + "1,1,1,1,1,1,1,1
" * N          # chunk 1 -> int64     + f"{2**64 - 1},1,1,1,1,1,1,1
"   # chunk 2 -> uint64     + f"{2**64 - 2},1,1,1,1,1,1,1
" )  res = pd.read_csv(StringIO(data))["a"] exp = pd.read_csv(StringIO(data), low_memory=False)["a"]  assert exp.iloc[-1] != exp.iloc[-2] assert res.iloc[-1] != res.iloc[-2]  #  <- fails because of unwanted casting ```  In the `low_memory=True` case, we do dtype inference in chunks.  In cases where different chunks get different dtypes, the concat does a cast which can be lossy.  `low_memory=False` avoids that by doing the dtype inference on the whole column instead of in chunks.  The alternative I think we should consider is to detect when this casting occurs and then re-parse (with `usecols` restricted to the affected column) in the `low_memory=False` mode.  Then we get the correct result and don't need the user-facing keyword.  The downside is a perf penalty in these corner cases.  Passing `low_memory=False` disables the parallel path, which is what brought this to my attention.

titulo: DEPR: cache_dates in read_csv
corpo: A review of github code shows that cache_dates is the least-used keyword, with 8.4k uses (compared to 1.01M of dtype).  Moreover, the cases where `cache_dates=False` improves performance are fewer and fewer now that ISO cases get excluded by default.  I think we should deprecate the keyword and have a slightly simpler API.  cc @mroeschke

titulo: API: select_dtypes
corpo: We made a bunch of changes to select_dtypes in July.  I advocate reverting the most niche use cases to simplify the code.    Summarizing the support that was *added*:  1) Passing an ExtensionDtype class matches every instance of that dtype (instead of raising) 2) Passing a partially-specified IntervalDtype e.g. IntervalDtype(np.int64) (without specifying "closed") matches all IntervalDtypes that match that partial specification. 3) Passing a partially-specified CategoricalDtype e.g. CategoricalDtype(my_categories, ordered=None) matches all CategoricalDtypes with those categories regardless of orderedness.  Summarizing the behavior that *changed* as bugfixes  4) Passing a specific dtype e.g. `np.dtype(np.int64)` matches exactly that dtype, not every integer dtype. 5) Passing a type (that isn't an ExtesnsionDtype subclass) raises instead of matching object dtype. 6) Passing EADtypes like Int64Dtype() would match numpy integer dtypes.  Summarizing deprecations  7) Deprecated accepting "datetimetz" and "datetime64tz" since item 1 now means you can pass pd.DatetimeTZDtype explicitly.  I advocate reverting items 2 and 3 before 3.1 is released, as they contribute a lot of complexity for very niche use cases.  Also we don't have a mechanism to do similar partial-specification matching for DatetimeTZDtype or 3rd party EAs.

titulo: BUG: parallel read_csv with sqlite converters
corpo:
@jbrockmendel  san
 I couldn't open a bug report because the form requires confirmation that the bug exists in the latest stable release. This parallel path is only on main and is not included in pandas 3.0.5, so I couldn't truthfully check that box. I'm reporting it here instead.
 
 I found an issue in the parallel read_csv path when using converters=. On the official 3.1.0.dev0+1870.g27449ca07b nightly, a stateful converter produced different results with mode.max_threads=4 and mode.max_threads=1.
 
 A converter using a SQLite connection created on the main thread also worked with mode.max_threads=1, but failed with mode.max_threads=4:
 
 ProgrammingError: SQLite objects created in a thread can only be used in that same thread.
 
 It looks like converters are being called from worker threads. Since parallel reads are expected to produce the same result as serial reads, I think read_csv should probably fall back to the serial path when converters is set.
 
 
 Could someone open a tracking issue for this, or let me know where main-only regressions should be reported? The bug report form cannot be submitted unless I confirm that the bug exists in the latest stable release.

titulo: ENH: move the postgresql extra from psycopg2 to psycopg 3
corpo: ### Feature Type  - [ ] Adding new functionality to pandas  - [x] Changing existing functionality in pandas  - [ ] Removing existing functionality in pandas   ### Problem Description  `pip install pandas[postgresql]` still installs psycopg2. Current pin on main, in `[project.optional-dependencies]`:      postgresql = ['SQLAlchemy>=2.0.42', 'psycopg2>=2.9.10', 'adbc-driver-postgresql>=1.7.0']  After #67968 the SQL user guide names psycopg 3 as the example SQLAlchemy driver for PostgreSQL, so the packaging and the docs now point at different generations of the driver. This came up in the review of that PR: https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/pull/67968#discussion_r3984002256  I wish `pandas[postgresql]` installed the driver the docs recommend.  ### Feature Description  Swap `psycopg2>=2.9.10` for a `psycopg` (3.x) pin with an appropriate floor, moving the coupled spots together:  - the `postgresql` extra in `pyproject.toml` - the `all` extra in `pyproject.toml` (same psycopg2 pin today) - `environment.yml` - the optional-dependencies table in `doc/source/getting_started/install.rst`   (lists psycopg2 as the PostgreSQL engine for SQLAlchemy)  The psycopg project describes psycopg2 as fully supported for legacy applications and recommends psycopg 3 for new projects. One compatibility question decides the floor and the shape of the change: in SQLAlchemy, psycopg2 remains the default dialect for bare `postgresql://` URLs, so replacing the pin changes what a fresh `pandas[postgresql]` install can connect with unless the engine string is explicit.  ### Alternative Solutions  - Ship both drivers in the extra (`psycopg` and `psycopg2`): no breakage   for users relying on psycopg2 being pulled in, at the cost of a heavier   install. The two packages coexist and SQLAlchemy picks the dialect from   the URL scheme. - Keep psycopg2 and treat the docs recommendation and the extra as   separate concerns; the user guide already shows both dialect strings   explicitly. - Replace psycopg2 with psycopg and accept that bare `postgresql://`   users must add psycopg2 themselves or move to the explicit   `postgresql+psycopg` scheme shown in the user guide.  ### Additional Context  - Raised by @jbrockmendel  in the review of #67968 (link above). - psycopg project statement: "Psycopg 2 remains fully supported for legacy   applications. New projects should use Psycopg 3." (psycopg.org) - SQLAlchemy 2.0 dialect docs: psycopg2 "remains the default dialect for   the `postgresql://` dialect series"; psycopg 3 requires the explicit   `postgresql+psycopg` scheme. - I run the explicit `postgresql+psycopg` path in production (pipeline   loading ~46M rows per day into PostgreSQL/TimescaleDB, psycopg 3.3.4   with SQLAlchemy 2.0.52 against PostgreSQL 17).

titulo: BUG: mixed int64/float64 Index operations falsely match distinct labels above 2**53
corpo: ### Pandas version checks  - [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.  - [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.  - [ ] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.   ### Reproducible Example  ```python import pandas as pd  integer_label = 2**53 + 1                  # 9007199254740993 float_label = float(2**53)                 # 9007199254740992.0  integer_index = pd.Index([integer_label], dtype="int64") float_index = pd.Index([float_label], dtype="float64")  print(integer_label == float_label) print("equals:", integer_index.equals(float_index))  try:     integer_index.get_loc(float_label) except KeyError:     print("get_loc: KeyError")  print("get_indexer:", integer_index.get_indexer(float_index)) print("intersection:", integer_index.intersection(float_index)) print("union:", integer_index.union(float_index)) print("difference:", integer_index.difference(float_index))  values = pd.Series(["payload"], index=integer_index) print("reindex:") print(values.reindex(float_index))  left = pd.Series([1], index=integer_index) right = pd.Series([2], index=float_index) print("aligned addition:") print(left + right)   Output on pandas 3.0.5:   False equals: True get_loc: KeyError get_indexer: [0] intersection: Index([9007199254740993], dtype='int64') union: Index([9007199254740992.0], dtype='float64') difference: Index([], dtype='int64') reindex: 9.007199e+15    payload dtype: str aligned addition: 9007199254740993    3 dtype: int64 ```  ### Issue Description  The two labels are distinct: Python equality returns `False`, and scalar `Index.get_loc` raises `KeyError`. However, `get_indexer` returns `[0]`. False matches also occur in Index set operations, reindexing, and arithmetic alignment.  This is not a case where the original integer has already been lost inside a float. The float label is exactly `2**53`, while the integer label is exactly `2**53 + 1`. They become equal only after the integer Index is cast to `float64` during mixed-dtype reconciliation.  Source inspection identifies more than one relevant path. For mismatched `int64`/`float64` dtypes, `get_indexer` calls `_find_common_type_compat`, casts both operands to `float64`, and then calls `_get_indexer`. This conversion rounds `2**53 + 1` to `2**53`.  Separately, `Index.equals` compares the underlying arrays through `array_equivalent` and returns `True` for these two Index objects. Both `intersection` and `difference` have early-return paths based on `Index.equals`, before their general matching logic. The observed results should therefore not all be attributed solely to `get_indexer`.  The practical consequence is silent association of data with a different label. Large numeric identifiers, transaction numbers, or similar keys can reach this path when one source uses `int64` and another uses `float64`, for example after an import or missing-value-driven conversion.  Related but distinct: #61676 and #66794 concern false matches in `isin`. That path now returns `False` for this pair on current main, while `get_indexer`, set operations, reindexing, and alignment still produce the results above. Merge dtype/precision reports such as #8596 and #61688 concern different APIs.  I found no identical public Issue or PR in searches for the concrete value `9007199254740993`, `2**53`, mixed `int64`/`float64` Index operations, and `get_indexer`. This does not guarantee that no duplicate exists.  ### Automated tools disclosure  I used OpenAI Codex (GPT-5; reasoning-effort setting not exposed) for English translation and formatting of this report. I reviewed the final issue text before submission.  ### Expected Behavior  Mixed numeric Index operations should not match labels that are unequal before dtype reconciliation. For the example above:  ```text integer_index.get_indexer(float_index) -> array([-1]) integer_index.intersection(float_index) -> empty Index integer_index.union(float_index) -> two distinct labels integer_index.difference(float_index) -> the original integer label values.reindex(float_index) -> missing value, not "payload" left + right -> two distinct labels with missing values ```  The exact result dtype for operations that must contain both labels may require a compatibility decision, but both exact values must be preserved as distinct labels.  ### Installed Versions  <details>  ```text INSTALLED VERSIONS ------------------ commit                : e68db09ecf6427d1b62e565bacf17f2e525a3032 python                : 3.12.10 python-bits           : 64 OS                    : Windows OS-release            : 11 Version               : 10.0.26200 machine               : AMD64 processor             : AMD64 Family 23 Model 8 Stepping 2, AuthenticAMD byteorder             : little 2.9.0.post0 pip                   : 26.2.1 Cython                : 3.3.0 pytest                : 9.1.1 sphinx                : None IPython               : None adbc-driver-postgresql: None adbc-driver-sqlite    : None bs4                   : None bottleneck            : None fastparquet           : None fsspec                : None html5lib              : None hypothesis            : None gcsfs                 : None jinja2                : None lxml.etree            : None matplotlib            : None numba                 : None numexpr               : None odfpy installation. Current main `a183ef5779ecce1a5f3d6b766e130cf860afdfaf` has the same affected `Index.get_indexer`, `Index.equals`, `Index.intersection`, `Index.difference`, `Index.union`, and `_find_common_type_compat` code paths. corpo: ### Pandas version checks  - [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.  - [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.  - [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.   ### Reproducible Example  ```python import numpy as np import pandas as pd  values = [0.0, np.nan] dense = pd.Series(values) sparse = pd.Series(pd.arrays.SparseArray(values, fill_value=0.0)) frame = sparse.to_frame("a")  print(sparse.any()) print(sparse.any(skipna=True)) print(dense.any(skipna=True))  print(sparse.any(skipna=False)) print(dense.any(skipna=False))  print(frame.any(skipna=True)["a"]) print(frame.any(skipna=False)["a"])   Output:   True True False False True True False ```  ### Issue Description  For `float64` data containing `np.nan`, `Series.any` gives the opposite `skipna` behavior when the Series is backed by a `SparseArray`. `DataFrame.any` shows the same behavior for a single `SparseArray`-backed column with the default `axis=0`. With `skipna=True`, the missing value is retained and makes the result `True`. With `skipna=False`, the missing value is dropped and the result becomes `False`.  This is a silent result difference from an equivalent dense Series. It also affects the default call, because `Series.any()` defaults to `skipna=True`.  The behavior appears to come from the non-skipna-aware branch of `SparseArray._reduce`, which currently selects the original array when `skipna=True` and calls `dropna()` when `skipna=False`:  ```python if skipna:     arr = self else:     arr = self.dropna() ```  Related but distinct work: #65478 concerns `SparseArray.mean` accepting `skipna`, and #68194 adds other SparseArray reductions. Neither appears to cover the reversed `Series.any` results above.  The reversed preprocessing branch appears to date back to commit `56d8e789155231b04131c6bf4674971ec3f38f95` (#22325, October 13, 2018), which made `SparseArray` an `ExtensionArray` and added `SparseArray._reduce`. It is present in the v0.24.0 source and in every sampled release line through 3.0.5, as well as current main. The first release containing it appears to be pandas 0.24.0.  ### Automated tools disclosure  I used OpenAI Codex (GPT-5; reasoning-effort setting not exposed) for English translation and formatting of this report. I reviewed the final issue text before submission.  ### Expected Behavior  The sparse and dense Series should return the same results:  ```text sparse.any()             -> False sparse.any(skipna=True)  -> False sparse.any(skipna=False) -> True frame.any(skipna=True)   -> False frame.any(skipna=False)  -> True ```  Equivalently, the non-skipna-aware preprocessing should drop titulo: BUG: IntervalIndex set ops and astype/constructor raise TypeError when passed a RangeIndex
corpo: ### Pandas version checks  - [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.  - [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.  - [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.  ### Reproducible Example  ```python import pandas as pd  iv = pd.IntervalIndex.from_breaks([0, 2, 4])  iv.union(pd.RangeIndex(0)) # TypeError: Argument 'intervals' has incorrect type (expected numpy.ndarray, got RangeIndex)  iv.symmetric_difference(pd.RangeIndex(0)) # TypeError: Argument 'intervals' has incorrect type (expected numpy.ndarray, got RangeIndex)  pd.RangeIndex(0).union(iv) # TypeError: Argument 'intervals' has incorrect type (expected numpy.ndarray, got RangeIndex)  pd.IntervalIndex(pd.RangeIndex(0)) # TypeError: Argument 'intervals' has incorrect type (expected numpy.ndarray, got RangeIndex)  pd.IntervalIndex(pd.RangeIndex(2, 4)) # TypeError: Argument 'intervals' has incorrect type (expected numpy.ndarray, got RangeIndex) ```  ### Issue Description  The same operations succeed with any other empty array-like, e.g.:  ```python iv.union(pd.Index([], dtype="int64"))   # IntervalIndex([(0, 2], (2, 4]], dtype='interval[int64, right]') iv.union(np.array([], dtype=np.int64))  # OK iv.union(pd.Series([], dtype="int64"))  # OK iv.union([])                            # OK ```  A non-empty ``RangeIndex`` with incompatible dtype also works (falls back to object dtype): ``iv.union(pd.RangeIndex(2, 4))`` -> ``Index([(0, 2], (2, 4], 2, 3], dtype='object')``.  Only ``RangeIndex`` arguments crash, both empty and non-empty (in the direct constructor), on both the LHS and RHS of set operations.  **Root cause** (observed on main, ``cb13b0e9a4``): in ``pandas/core/arrays/interval.py``, ``_maybe_convert_platform_interval`` only converts ``values`` to an ndarray when it lacks a ``dtype`` attribute:  ```python if not hasattr(values, "dtype"):     values = np.asarray(values) ```  ``RangeIndex`` has a ``dtype``, so it is passed through unchanged to the Cython function ``intervals_to_interval_bounds``, which requires an ndarray and raises ``TypeError: Argument 'intervals' has incorrect type (expected numpy.ndarray, got RangeIndex)``.  Trigger paths: 1. Direct: ``pd.IntervalIndex(RangeIndex(...))`` / ``IntervalArray(RangeIndex(...))`` / ``RangeIndex.astype("interval")``. 2. Set ops: ``IntervalIndex.union`` with an empty ``other`` where ``_find_common_type_compat(other)`` resolves to ``interval[int64, right]`` (empty ``RangeIndex``; an empty ``Index`` instead resolves to ``object``), then ``other.astype(interval_dtype)`` raises before the empty-``other`` short-circuit is reached.  ### Expected Behavior  Set operations between an ``IntervalIndex`` and an empty ``RangeIndex`` should behave like the other empty array-likes (union/symmetric_difference return the original interval index), and constructing an ``IntervalIndex`` from a ``RangeIndex`` should either work consistently or raise the regular ``TypeError: ... is not an interval`` message (matching ``pd.IntervalIndex([2, 3])``), not a Cython ``TypeError`` about internal argument types.  A fix converting ``RangeIndex`` to an ndarray in ``_maybe_convert_platform_interval`` (as is already done for empty lists, ``GH19016``) resolves all of the cases above.  ### Installed Versions  <details>  INSTALLED VERSIONS ------------------ commit                : cb13b0e9a4 python                : 3.12.4 python-bits           : 64 OS                    : Windows OS-release            : 11 machine               : AMD64 pandas                : 3.1.0.dev0+1815.gcb13b0e9a4 numpy                 : 2.5.1  </details>  Reproduced on the released wheels of pandas 3.0.3 as well.

titulo: BUG: Series/DataFrame.replace with a callable value silently stores the function instead of applying or rejecting it
corpo: Passing a callable as `value` to `replace` stores the function object as the replacement data. It neither applies it nor raises:  ```python s = pd.Series(["a1", "b2"]) s.replace(r"\d", lambda m: "X", regex=True) # 0    <function <lambda> at 0x...> # 1    <function <lambda> at 0x...> ```  Same for exact match without regex and for `DataFrame.replace`. Reproduced on 3.0.5.  `Series.str.replace` with the same arguments returns `["aX", "bX"]`, and the `replace` docs list `value` as scalar/dict/list/str/regex with no callables. GH#18634 set the precedent that invalid `replace` arguments raise, and the suite tests a callable `to_replace` raising, but nothing covers a callable `value`. On main (`pandas/core/generic.py`, `replace`), `to_replace` is validated up front and `value` is not checked at all.  The corruption spreads silently: the result is object dtype holding functions, `to_json` renders them as `{}`, and later string ops fail far from the mistake (`TypeError: expected string or bytes-like object, got 'function'`). Support callables or raise like `to_replace` does. Storing them should not happen.

titulo: BUG: read_csv fails to finalize index when engine='pyarrow' and dtype is scalar (or dict without an index specified)
corpo:
### Pandas version checks - [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported. - [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas. - [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas. ### Reproducible Example ```python from io import StringIO test=""" col1,col2 10,1 20,2 """ f=StringIO(test) import pandas as pd import pyarrow as pa # For AttributeError df = pd.read_csv( f, dtype='int64[pyarrow]', dtype_backend='pyarrow', engine='pyarrow', # Removing either engine or index_col avoids the error index_col='col1', ) # For IndexError df = pd.read_csv( f, dtype={'col2': 'int64[pyarrow]'}, dtype_backend='pyarrow', engine='pyarrow', # Removing either engine or index_col avoids the error index_col='col1', ) print(df.info()) # Simplified example here; see below for more complete testing results ``` ### Issue Description Using `read_csv` raises an `AttributeError` if... - `index_col` is specified, and - `engine='pyarrow'` is specified, and - `dtype` is specified as a scalar or a `dict` that doesn't include the index column ### Scenario A: Scalar dtype raises AttributeError The AttributeError occurs in `ArrowParserWrapper._finalize_index` ([3.0.5](https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/e68db09ecf6427d1b62e565bacf17f2e525a3032/pandas/io/parsers/arrow_parser_wrapper.py#L202) | [main](https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/795cd84559d9147679bfe8461853569727a5ee69/pandas/io/parsers/arrow_parser_wrapper.py#L390)) when it tries to call `self.dtype.get(item)` on a scalar dtype (e.g., 'int64[pyarrow]' or pd.ArrowDtype(pa.int64())) instead of a dictionary.
Simplified traceback of AttributeError ``` File "deleteme.py", line 10, in df = pd.read_csv( f, ...<3 lines>... index_col='col1', # Works fine if removed ) File "....\site-packages\pandas\io\parsers\readers.py", line 873, in read_csv return _read(filepath_or_buffer, kwds) File "....\site-packages\pandas\io\parsers\readers.py", line 306, in _read return parser.read(nrows) ~~~~~~~~~~~^^^^^^^ File "....\site-packages\pandas\io\parsers\readers.py", line 1935, in read df = self._engine.read() # type: ignore[attr-defined] File "....\site-packages\pandas\io\parsers\arrow_parser_wrapper.py", line 328, in read return self._finalize_pandas_output(frame, multi_index_named) ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ File "....\site-packages\pandas\io\parsers\arrow_parser_wrapper.py", line 253, in _finalize_pandas_output frame = self._finalize_index(frame, multi_index_named) File "....\site-packages\pandas\io\parsers\arrow_parser_wrapper.py", line 202, in _finalize_index if self.dtype.get(item) is not None ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ AttributeError: 'str' object has no attribute 'get' ```
### Scenario B: Dictionary dtype missing the index column raises IndexError If a dictionary is passed to `dtype` but the index column is omitted from the keys, it looks like the wrapper engine incorrectly handles the remaining columns during `_finalize_dtype`, leading to an `IndexError` down the line.
Simplified traceback of IndexError ``` File "....\site-packages\pandas\io\parsers\readers.py", line 873, in read_csv return _read(filepath_or_buffer, kwds) File "....\site-packages\pandas\io\parsers\readers.py", line 306, in _read return parser.read(nrows) ~~~~~~~~~~~^^^^^^^ File "....\site-packages\pandas\io\parsers\readers.py", line 1935, in read df = self._engine.read() # type: ignore[attr-defined] File "....\site-packages\pandas\io\parsers\arrow_parser_wrapper.py", line 328, in read return self._finalize_pandas_output(frame, multi_index_named) ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ File "....\site-packages\pandas\io\parsers\arrow_parser_wrapper.py", line 253, in _finalize_pandas_output frame = self._finalize_index(frame, multi_index_named) File "....\site-packages\pandas\io\parsers\arrow_parser_wrapper.py", line 203, in _finalize_index else (frame.columns[item], self.dtype.get(frame.columns[item])) ~~~~~~~~~~~~~^^^^^^ File "....\site-packages\pandas\core\indexes\base.py", line 5425, in __getitem__ result = getitem(key) File "....\site-packages\pandas\core\arrays\arrow\array.py", line 780, in __getitem__ raise IndexError( ...<2 lines>... ) IndexError: only integers, slices (`:`), ellipsis (`...`), numpy.newaxis (`None`) and integer or boolean arrays are valid indices ```

titulo: BUG: addition of non-UTC DatetimeArray with large Timedelta returns None
corpo: With tz-naive (or UTC), this works fine: ```python >>> arr = pd.array([0, 86400], dtype="M8[s]") >>> arr <DatetimeArray> ['1970-01-01 00:00:00', '1970-01-02 00:00:00'] Length: 2, dtype: datetime64[s] >>> arr + np.timedelta64(10**13, "s") <DatetimeArray> ['318857-05-20 17:46:40', '318857-05-21 17:46:40'] Length: 2, dtype: datetime64[s] ```  But when the array has a non-UTC timezone, it just returns nothing (`None`): ```python >>> arr = pd.array([0, 86400], dtype="M8[s, Europe/Brussels]") >>> arr + np.timedelta64(10**13, "s") >>> arr + pd.Timedelta(np.timedelta64(10**13, "s")) ```  This happens on main, and also on 3.0.5, but worked fine on 2.3. So this seems a regression compared to 2.x.

titulo: BUILD: window/meson.build never passes --shared=pandas._libs._cyutility to its extensions
corpo: `pandas/_libs/window/meson.build` opens with  ```meson cy_args = ['-X always_allow_keywords=true'] # Use shared utility code to reduce wheel sizes # copied from https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/31151/files if cy.version().version_compare('>=3.1.0')     cython_args += ['--shared=pandas._libs._cyutility'] endif ```  but both `py.extension_module` calls in that file pass `cython_args: cy_args`. The `+=` lands on `cython_args`, the variable inherited from `pandas/_libs/meson.build` (which already appends the same flag there), so the flag never reaches `pandas._libs.window.aggregations` or `pandas._libs.window.indexers` — each of them still emits its own copy of the Cython utility code. The append also mutates the inherited variable as a side effect, which is not what the surrounding code intends.  `cy_args` is also missing the `--include-dir` pair that `pandas/_libs/meson.build` puts in `cython_args`.  Introduced by GH-61384 (341f1612a98). Impact is wheel size only — no correctness effect.  Fix: pass the shared flag to the window extensions, e.g. append to `cy_args` rather than `cython_args` (or reuse the parent `cython_args` directly if the `--include-dir` entries are wanted here too).

titulo: BUILD: pyproject.toml banned-api comment is wrong — TID251 does resolve np.random through the alias
corpo: `pyproject.toml` carries this in `[tool.ruff.lint.flake8-tidy-imports.banned-api]`:  ```toml # numpy.random is banned but np.random is not. Is this intentional? # "numpy.random".msg = "Do not use numpy.random" ```  The premise is false. TID251 resolves qualified names through aliased module imports, so with `import numpy as np` a `"numpy.random"` entry does flag `np.random.rand()` at the call site. Verified against ruff 0.15.7 and the pinned 0.16.1:  ```toml [tool.ruff.lint.flake8-tidy-imports.banned-api] "numpy.random".msg = "no np.random" ```  ```python import numpy as np np.random.rand()   # -> TID251 `numpy.random` is banned ```  So either the commented-out entry can simply be uncommented — pandas already forbids unseeded `default_rng()` / `np.random` in tests via a pygrep hook in `.pre-commit-config.yaml`, which this would partly subsume — or, at minimum, the misleading comment should be deleted so nobody re-derives it.

titulo: TST: pandas/tests/api/test_api.py::TestApi::test_api fails when that directory is run on its own
corpo: `TestApi.allowed_api_dirs` in `pandas/tests/api/test_api.py` lists `"internals"`, and `test_api` compares that list against `dir(pandas.api)`. But `pandas/api/__init__.py` does not import the `internals` submodule, and a submodule only shows up in its parent's `dir()` once something has imported it. So the test passes only when an earlier test in the same process has done that — in practice `pandas/tests/internals/test_api.py`.  Run the directory on its own and it fails:  ``` $ pytest pandas/tests/api/test_api.py -p no:randomly FAILED pandas/tests/api/test_api.py::TestApi::test_api - AssertionError: Iterable are different  Iterable length are different [left]:  6 [right]: 7 [diff]: ['internals'] ```  ```python import pandas as pd "internals" in dir(pd.api)   # False import pandas.api.internals "internals" in dir(pd.api)   # True ```  `pandas/api/internals.py` exists and is tracked; this is purely about whether it has been imported.  Not a CI risk today (CI runs the whole suite), but it makes running that one directory locally look broken, and the test is only green because of what its neighbours happened to do first.  Fix is one of:  1. import `internals` from `pandas/api/__init__.py` — it is public API, so arguably `pd.api.internals` should be reachable off a bare `import pandas`; 2. import it in the test before checking; or 3. drop it from `allowed_api_dirs` and assert it separately.  Choosing between them is really a question about whether `pd.api.internals` is meant to be reachable without an explicit import.

titulo: BUG: find_stack_level treats third-party `pandas*` packages as pandas-internal
corpo:
### Problem  `find_stack_level` (`pandas/util/_exceptions.py`) walks the stack while  ```python filename.startswith(pkg_dir) and not filename.startswith(test_dir) ```  `pkg_dir` is `os.path.dirname(pandas.__file__)`, e.g. `.../site-packages/pandas`, with no trailing `os.sep`. So `.../site-packages/pandas_ta/strategy.py` matches too, and the walk keeps climbing past it. Every sibling distribution whose install directory merely *starts with* `pandas` — `pandas_ta`, `pandas_gbq`, `pandas_datareader`, `pandasql`, ... — is invisible to the walk, so warnings raised on behalf of user code in those packages get a `stacklevel` that points past the real caller.  ### Reproducible example  No third-party package needed; only the filename matters.  ```python import warnings  import pandas.util._exceptions as pue  pue.find_stack_level()  # populate the cache pkg_dir = pue._pkg_dir  src = (     "import warnings
"     "from pandas.util._exceptions import find_stack_level
"     "def caller():
"     "    warnings.warn('boom', UserWarning, stacklevel=find_stack_level())
" )  for path in (pkg_dir + "_ta/strategy.py", "/somewhere/else/strategy.py"):     ns = {}     exec(compile(src, path, "exec"), ns)     with warnings.catch_warnings(record=True) as rec:         warnings.simplefilter("always")         ns["caller"]()     print(f"{path}
  -> reported at {rec[0].filename}:{rec[0].lineno}") ```  ``` /.../site-packages/pandas_ta/strategy.py   -> reported at repro.py:22            # wrong: skipped past the warning site /somewhere/else/strategy.py   -> reported at /somewhere/else/strategy.py:4   # correct ```  The consequence is sharper anywhere the *return value* is used as a decision rather than just a pointer (e.g. suppressing a warning when `find_stack_level()` exceeds some depth): user code living in such a package can end up getting no warning at all.  ### Suggested fix  Cache `_pkg_dir` as `os.path.dirname(pd.__file__) + os.sep` (and `_test_dir` likewise) so the comparison is directory-scoped. One line, no new imports.  Expect some churn: tightening the walk shifts stacklevels across the codebase, and `pandas/_testing/_warnings.py::_assert_raised_with_correct_stacklevel` asserts the reported filename, so a full test run is needed to see what moves.

titulo: TST: test_duplicated_hashtable_impl monkeypatches _SIZE_CUTOFF on a path that never reads it
corpo: `pandas/tests/indexes/multi/test_duplicates.py::test_duplicated_hashtable_impl` wraps its assertions in  ```python with monkeypatch.context() as m:     m.setattr(libindex, "_SIZE_CUTOFF", 50) ```  but nothing on the path under test reads `_SIZE_CUTOFF`. `MultiIndex.duplicated` is `get_group_index` + `hashtable.duplicated` on the codes — it never constructs an index engine:  ```python import numpy as np from pandas import MultiIndex from pandas._libs import index as libindex, hashtable  n, k = 6, 10 levels = [np.arange(n), [str(i) for i in range(n)], 1000 + np.arange(n)] rng = np.random.default_rng(2) codes = [rng.choice(n, k * n) for _ in levels] mi = MultiIndex(levels=levels, codes=codes)  mi.duplicated(keep="first") hashtable.duplicated(mi.values, keep="first") print("_engine" in mi._cache)   # False - no engine is ever built print(libindex._SIZE_CUTOFF)    # 1000000 unpatched; results are identical either way ```  It is inert twice over: even if an engine *were* built, `_SIZE_CUTOFF` only feeds `IndexEngine.__init__` and `ExtensionEngine.__init__` in `index.pyx`. `BaseMultiIndexCodesEngine` has no `over_size_threshold` member at all, so no MultiIndex engine has ever consulted the cutoff.  Provenance: the test was `test_duplicated_large` at `n, k = 200, 5000` (1,000,000 rows). GH-53862 shrank it to 60 rows, added the monkeypatch to preserve what it read as the "large" path, and renamed it `_hashtable_impl`. But `MultiIndex.duplicated` has gone through `get_group_index` + `hashtable.duplicated` since GH-27647 / GH-40944 at least, so the engine was never on the path the old size was buying either — the rename named a code path the test has never touched.  Suggested fix: drop the `monkeypatch.context()` block and the `monkeypatch` fixture argument, and rename the test to what it actually asserts — that the codes-based `MultiIndex.duplicated` agrees with `hashtable.duplicated` over the tuple values. Real coverage of the over-cutoff engine would be a separate test against an engine that reads the cutoff.

titulo: BENCH: ChainIndexing benchmark no longer measures chained assignment
corpo: `ChainIndexing` in `asv_bench/benchmarks/indexing.py` was written to measure the `SettingWithCopy` bookkeeping — hence the `params = [None, "warn"]` A/B over `mode.chained_assignment` and the `catch_warnings` around the body. `SettingWithCopyWarning` was removed in GH-56614, so both of those became no-ops; GH-67987 drops them, leaving:  ```python class ChainIndexing:     def setup(self):         self.N = 1000000         self.df = DataFrame({"A": np.arange(self.N), "B": "foo"})      def time_chained_indexing(self):         df = self.df         N = self.N         df2 = df[df.A > N // 2]         df2["C"] = 1.0 ```  I think what remains should just be deleted, for three reasons.  **It does not touch the machinery it is named after.** The guard in `DataFrame.__setitem__` is  ```python if sys.getrefcount(self) <= REF_COUNT and not com.is_local_in_caller_frame(self): ```  Because the benchmark binds `df2` to a name, the refcount test is false and short-circuits, so `is_local_in_caller_frame` is never called. Counting calls: 0 for the benchmark as written, 1 for a genuinely chained `df[df.A > N // 2]["C"] = 1.0`.  **What is left is already covered.** Timing the pieces on a 1M-row frame:  ``` mask only (== DataFrameIndexing.time_boolean_rows)   3.34 ms ChainIndexing (current)                              3.50 ms ```  95% of it is the boolean mask, measured by `DataFrameIndexing.time_boolean_rows`; the residual column assign is covered by `InsertColumns.time_assign_with_setitem`.  **Making it genuinely chained would not rescue it.** The chained form measures 3.45 ms against the current 3.50 ms — no signal, because the frame walk is ~0.1% of a 1M-row mask. Shrinking the frame does not expose it either; at N=100 the chained-vs-named delta is +0.3 us against a 122 us baseline.  So the benchmark was only ever meaningful as the `[None, "warn"]` comparison, and there is no residual question it answers.  Separately: the per-assignment cost of the refcount + `is_local_in_caller_frame` check is real and currently untracked — GH-66318 cited ~4 us per assignment inside compiled callers. If that is worth an ASV benchmark it wants a purpose-built one (tiny frame, isolating the `__setitem__` call, no mask), not a repurposing of this one.  AI disclosure: drafted with Claude Code (`claude opus 5 (high)`), which took the measurements and the call-count instrumentation above.

titulo: CI: sanitizers environment has no pyarrow, so the read_csv pyarrow string path is never sanitized
corpo: The `sanitizers` environment has no pyarrow, so the one CI job that builds with `-Db_sanitize=address,undefined` cannot reach the `read_csv` pyarrow-backed string path at all.  `pixi.toml`:  ```toml sanitizers = { features = ["py313", "numpy", "test-base", "optional-dependencies", "sanitizers"] } ```  `optional-dependencies` does not include pyarrow, and every other test environment lists it as its own feature (`pyarrow22`, `pyarrow23`, `pyarrow24`, `pyarrow`). The only other environment that omits it is `no-pyarrow`, where that is the entire point. `pixi.lock` confirms it: no pyarrow and no libarrow anywhere in the `sanitizers` environment.  The consequence is that `_string_pyarrow_utf8` is dead code in that job. `_string_convert` gates the fast path on `HAS_PYARROW` (`pandas/_libs/parsers.pyx:1545`), and the string tests `importorskip("pyarrow")`, so under the sanitizer both the code and its tests are skipped.  That path is the one most in need of ASAN, because its failure mode is invisible to every other kind of test. It deliberately over-reads each token by up to 32 bytes into reserved slack:  ``` cdef enum:     # Bytes of slack `_string_pyarrow_utf8` reserves past the end of its data     # buffer so `_copy_token` can round short copies up to a fixed width.     WILDCOPY_SLACK = 32 ```  A wrong `wild_limit` offset, a dropped `+ WILDCOPY_SLACK`, or an undersized capacity clamp produces no wrong values whatsoever — only a heap read outside the object, which is exactly and only what ASAN detects. Concretely: while three separate real memory-sizing bugs were present in this code, four rounds of differential fuzzing against the object path found zero value mismatches. Sanitizer coverage is the only thing that would have caught them, and it is precisely what this environment cannot provide.  Two related gaps in the same vein: `py313-freethreading` and `numpy-nightly` are also pyarrow-free, so the deferred/threaded string path has no free-threading coverage either.  The fix is to add `"pyarrow"` to those feature lists and relock. Worth flagging up front that this may surface pre-existing sanitizer failures elsewhere — pyarrow pulls in a large amount of native code that has never been run in this job — so it is plausibly two steps: turn it on, see what falls out, then decide what to suppress versus fix.

titulo: BUG: validate_test_dependencies.py is blind to pixi [target.*.dependencies]
corpo: `scripts/validate_test_dependencies.py` (pre-commit hook `validate-test-dependencies`) checks that every module gated by `pytest.importorskip` / `td.skip_if_no` is installed in at least one pixi environment that runs the test suite.  `declared_packages` builds that set from `pixi["dependencies"]` plus, per environment, `pixi["feature"][f]["dependencies"]` and `["pypi-dependencies"]`. It never reads the top-level `[target.<platform>.dependencies]` tables. `pixi.toml` has one today:  ```toml [target.win.dependencies] tzdata = ">=2023.3" ```  So a gate on a platform-scoped dependency gets reported as  ``` 'tzdata' gates tests with importorskip/skip_if_no, but 'tzdata' is not installed in any environment that runs the test suite, so these tests never run: ```  which is false as written — it *is* installed, on Windows. There is no such gate on main right now, so this is latent rather than currently firing, but it will fire the moment someone adds one, and the failure mode is a pre-commit hook telling the author something untrue about their own diff.  The underlying warning is still worth having: a Windows-only gate does mean the test is skipped on every Linux and macOS job, which is usually not what the author intended. So the fix is probably not to silence it but to parse the `[target.*.dependencies]` tables and reword — report *which* platforms the gate actually runs on, rather than claiming none. Distinguishing "runs nowhere" from "runs only on win" is the useful signal, and only the first should fail the hook.  No false negatives, only a misleading message on what is arguably a true positive.

titulo: TST: set LC_TIME in the test body instead of skipping under skip_if_not_english_lc_time
corpo: Follow-up to GH-67471, where this was raised in review and deferred ("OK in a follow up").  GH-67471 replaced `td.skip_if_not_us_locale` — which tested `locale.getlocale()[0] != "en_US"`, i.e. the *name* of `LC_CTYPE`, unrelated to what it was gating — with `td.skip_if_not_english_lc_time`, which probes `strftime` output directly:  ```python def _has_english_lc_time() -> bool:     stamp = datetime(2020, 1, 1, 13)  # a Wednesday     return stamp.strftime("%b|%B|%a|%A|%p") == "Jan|January|Wed|Wednesday|PM"  skip_if_not_english_lc_time = pytest.mark.skipif(     not _has_english_lc_time(),     reason="LC_TIME does not use English month names and AM/PM markers", ) ```  That is a strict improvement in accuracy, but it is still a skip: on a machine whose `LC_TIME` is not English, roughly 20 tests silently do not run.  They don't need to be skipped. The tests care about parsing/formatting English month names and AM/PM markers, so the test body can set `LC_TIME` for its own duration instead of declining to run:  - `pandas._config.localization.set_locale` is the context manager (it restores on exit). - `pandas._config.localization.can_set_locale` is the guard for whether an English locale is installed at all.  The decorator does not go away — it becomes "skip only if an English `LC_TIME` cannot be obtained" rather than "skip if the ambient one isn't English", which is a much smaller set of machines.  Sites, everything currently decorated with `@td.skip_if_not_english_lc_time`:  - `pandas/tests/extension/test_arrow.py` - `pandas/tests/frame/methods/test_between_time.py` - `pandas/tests/tools/test_to_datetime.py` - `pandas/tests/tools/test_to_time.py` - `pandas/tests/tslibs/test_parsing.py`  One constraint worth stating up front, because it is the reason GH-67471 existed: any test that calls `setlocale` must restore it. CPython sets only `LC_CTYPE` at startup, which is *why* a pandas process normally has English `LC_TIME` regardless of `LANG`; a test that leaves `LC_TIME` changed leaks into every later test in the process and recreates exactly the problem GH-67471 fixed. `set_locale` used as a context manager handles this.

titulo: CI: setup-pixi action's environment input description points at pyproject.toml, but the environments are in pixi.toml
corpo: `.github/actions/setup-pixi/action.yml:3-6`:  ```yaml inputs:   environment:     description: Pixi environment name in pyproject.toml to use.     required: true ```  pandas has no pixi configuration in `pyproject.toml` at all — no `[tool.pixi]`, no `[environments]`. Both `setup-pixi` invocations in this same file pass `manifest-path: pixi.toml`, and the `[environments]` table that actually defines `py311`…`py314`, `numpy-nightly`, `pyarrow-nightly`, `minimum-versions`, `doctests`, `typing`, `asv`, `docs-and-web` and the rest lives in `pixi.toml`.  So the one line that tells a reader where to find the legal values for this input sends them to a file that has none. The action's own `description:` on the line above already says "the environments section in pixi.toml".  Fix is one word:  ```yaml     description: Pixi environment name in pixi.toml to use. ```  The string dates to `61f964b10a8` ("CI: Use Pixi in CI unit test environments", GH-63969). Small enough to fold into whatever next touches this file.

titulo: CI: pixi-version is pinned in three places and dependabot bumps none of them
corpo: The pinned pixi version appears in three places, kept in sync only by hand:  ``` .github/actions/setup-pixi/action.yml:13   pixi-version: v0.76.2 .github/actions/setup-pixi/action.yml:24   pixi-version: v0.76.2 .github/workflows/update-pixi-lock.yml:28  pixi-version: v0.76.2 ```  Nothing links them, and dependabot does not bump them. It only rewrites the action reference: `git show aba3a606311` ("Bump prefix-dev/setup-pixi from 0.10.1 to 0.10.2") updates both `uses: prefix-dev/setup-pixi@...` lines and leaves all three `pixi-version` values untouched. So the pixi bump itself is manual (last done in `cae1cd626f8`, "CI: Update pixi to 0.76.2 + relock"), and editing one site without the others produces no error, no lint failure, and no diff anywhere else.  The two `action.yml` sites are the easy pair to get wrong, because they are the same action taking opposite branches of one condition — line 13 serves every environment except `pyarrow-nightly`, line 24 serves only `pyarrow-nightly`. Bumping one and not the other leaves that job installing under a different pixi than the rest of CI, and it is a job whose failures already tend to get dismissed as upstream nightly breakage.  Missing the third site is worse in kind, since `update-pixi-lock.yml` is what *writes* `pixi.lock`: a lock produced by a different pixi than the one consuming it is how lock-format skew gets committed.  Two ways to fix:  - **Pin once in the action.** Collapse `action.yml`'s two `setup-pixi` invocations into a single expression-driven step — `run-install`, `cache` and `environments` can all be derived from `inputs.environment == 'pyarrow-nightly'` — leaving one pin in the action and one in the relock workflow. This also removes the two mutually exclusive branches a reader currently has to hold in their head. It does depend on setup-pixi input-coercion behavior that isn't documented (an empty `environments` must coerce to unset so `validateInputs`' "Cannot specify environments without running install" doesn't fire), so it needs to be exercised in CI rather than reasoned about. - **Check instead of dedupe.** Leave the structure alone and add a pre-commit check that the three `pixi-version` values agree, alongside the existing pixi-related scripts in `scripts/`.

titulo: PERF: avoid per-element group labels in nullable DataFrame axis=1 reductions
corpo: ### Pandas version checks  - [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.  - [x] I have confirmed this issue exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.  - [x] I have confirmed this issue exists on the main branch of pandas.   ### Reproducible Example  The existing `axis=1` reduction path for homogeneous ExtensionArray-backed DataFrames concatenates the columns into a one-dimensional array. It then constructs the row labels with:  ```python row_index = np.tile(np.arange(nrows), ncols) ```  This creates one group label for every element in the DataFrame. The flattened values and labels are subsequently passed to `_groupby_op` with `ngroups=nrows`.  For supported nullable masked and Arrow numeric or Boolean arrays, the existing groupby kernels can instead operate on column-major data and mask buffers viewed as `(nrows, ncols)`. The specialized path requires only `ncols` zero-valued group IDs and one group. This retains the kernel and the ordering of columns within each row while avoiding the `nrows * ncols` label allocation.  The optimization applies to `sum`, `prod`, `min`, and `max`. Unsupported ExtensionArrays, Arrow subclasses and types, other operations, and empty DataFrames continue to use the existing path. Arrow numeric and Boolean arrays delegate through their corresponding masked representation before the result is reconstructed as an Arrow array. Public behavior is intended to remain unchanged.  The following reproducer uses four nullable integer columns, 100,000 rows, and approximately 10% missing values:  ```python from timeit import repeat  import numpy as np import pandas as pd   rng = np.random.default_rng(2) values = rng.integers(-100, 100, size=(100_000, 4)).astype(float) values[rng.random(values.shape) < 0.1] = np.nan df = pd.DataFrame(values).astype("Int64")   def best_ms(func):     return min(repeat(func, number=20, repeat=7)) / 20 * 1_000   print(f"pandas: {pd.__version__}") for name in ("sum", "prod", "min", "max"):     func = getattr(df, name)     print(f"{name}: {best_ms(lambda func=func: func(axis=1)):.3f} ms") ```  The configurations were run sequentially on the same compute node. Units are milliseconds, and lower is better.  ```text pandas 3.0.5: sum: 11.797 ms prod: 11.362 ms min: 12.847 ms max: 12.918 ms  upstream main (ebcf0ed7): sum: 3.214 ms prod: 2.358 ms min: 3.825 ms max: 3.918 ms  candidate branch (b011936d): sum: 1.760 ms prod: 1.305 ms min: 2.508 ms max: 2.650 ms ```  Relative to current `main`, these point estimates correspond to approximately:  * 45.2% lower runtime for `sum` * 44.7% lower runtime for `prod` * 34.4% lower runtime for `min` * 32.4% lower runtime for `max`  ### ASV results  The matched timing comparison was run on  an x86-64 machine with 96 Intel Xeon Platinum 8488C CPUs:  ```bash asv continuous upstream/main HEAD \   -E virtualenv:3.13 \   -f 1.1 \   --split \   --interleave-rounds \   -b FrameOpsAxis1EA.time_op ```  The 40-case benchmark grid covered:  * `sum`, `prod`, `min`, and `max` * `Int64`, `Float64`, `boolean`, `int64[pyarrow]`, and `float64[pyarrow]` * Shapes `(100_000, 4)` and `(1_000, 400)`  All 40 timing cases were classified as improvements at a significance factor of 1.1. Candidate-to-baseline ratios ranged from 0.38 to 0.86, with no unchanged or slower cases in this matched run.  Representative results:  ```text sum / boolean / (100000, 4): 5.39 ± 0.08 ms -> 2.10 ± 0.03 ms  (ratio 0.39)  prod / Int64 / (100000, 4): 2.50 ± 0.04 ms -> 1.41 ± 0.02 ms  (ratio 0.56)  min / float64[pyarrow] / (100000, 4): 4.85 ± 0.02 ms -> 3.73 ± 0.03 ms  (ratio 0.77)  max / int64[pyarrow] / (1000, 400): 4.51 ± 0.03 ms -> 3.62 ± 0.02 ms  (ratio 0.80)  prod / float64[pyarrow] / (1000, 400): 4.30 ± 0.07 ms -> 3.71 ± 0.02 ms  (ratio 0.86) ```  Peak memory was measured with:  ```bash asv continuous upstream/main HEAD \   -E virtualenv:3.13 \   -f 1.01 \   --split \   -b FrameOpsAxis1EAPeakmem.peakmem_op ```  For `(2_000_000, 5)` DataFrames:  ```text sum / Int64:             407 MB -> 363 MB  (ratio 0.89) max / Int64:             410 MB -> 363 MB  (ratio 0.89) sum / float64[pyarrow]:  434 MB -> 361 MB  (ratio 0.83) max / float64[pyarrow]:  417 MB -> 362 MB  (ratio 0.87) ```  ### Related work  This is a refinement of the ExtensionArray `axis=1` reduction path introduced in #54341 , rather than a new general row-reduction implementation. The narrower problem here is the tiled per-element group-label array used by that path.  Other related work includes:  * #51474  the broader request to improve `sum`, `prod`, `min`, and `max` with `axis=1`. * #56903 , which concerned Boolean row-wise `any` and `all`. This issue instead concerns `sum`, `prod`, `min`, and `max` on masked and Arrow numeric or Boolean dtypes. * #65105 and #67969, which concern the NumPy-backed multi-block path. This issue concerns homogeneous one-dimensional ExtensionArray columns and the group labels created after concatenating them.  ### Verification  The following test selections completed successfully:  * Focused selection: 437 passed. * `pandas.tests.frame.test_reductions`: 4,971 passed, 1,542 skipped, and 2 xfailed. * Eight related reduction, masked, integer, floating, Boolean, groupby, and transpose targets: 12,248 passed, 157 skipped, and 24 xfailed. * Full Arrow extension suite: 27,204 passed, 1,906 skipped, and 506 xfailed.  The non-double-counted total is 44,423 passing tests. The 437 focused cases are included in the full frame-module count.  All applicable configured pre-commit hooks passed on the five changed files. titulo: PERF: avoid temporary allocations in multi-block DataFrame axis=1 reductions
corpo: ### Pandas version checks  - [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.  - [x] I have confirmed this issue exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.  - [x] I have confirmed this issue exists on the main branch of pandas.   ## Reproducible Example  Multi-block `DataFrame` reductions along `axis=1` use the `_reduce_axis1` fast path for operations such as `sum`, `prod`, `min`, and `max`. For eligible NumPy-backed blocks, the current implementation still creates a per-block `middle` vector and then allocates another result while combining it with the accumulated reduction.  These intermediate allocations become significant for DataFrames with many rows and several blocks. For a guarded subset of compatible NumPy blocks, the reduction and combine steps can avoid these temporaries while retaining the existing fallback for other block types and configurations.  ```python from timeit import repeat  import numpy as np import pandas as pd   nrows = 1_000_000 rng = np.random.default_rng(2) df = pd.DataFrame(index=range(nrows)) for i in range(8):     values = rng.uniform(0.9, 1.1, nrows)     values[i::1000] = np.nan     df[f"column-{i}"] = values  assert len(df._mgr.blocks) == 8   def best_ms(func):     return min(repeat(func, number=5, repeat=7)) / 5 * 1_000   for name in ("sum", "prod", "min", "max"):     value = best_ms(lambda name=name: getattr(df, name)(axis=1))     print(f"{name}: {value:.3f} ms") ```  ```text pandas 3.0.5: sum: 141.387 ms prod: 147.783 ms min: 181.131 ms max: 185.854 ms  upstream main (ebcf0ed7): sum: 39.205 ms prod: 37.257 ms min: 18.315 ms max: 18.293 ms  optimized branch (40817a6d): sum: 26.450 ms prod: 26.643 ms min: 5.681 ms max: 5.696 ms ```  Compared with upstream main, the optimized implementation reduced runtime by approximately:  * 32.5% for `sum` * 28.5% for `prod` * 69.0% for `min` * 68.9% for `max`  A matched ASV comparison covered 72 cases across:  * `sum`, `prod`, `min`, and `max` * 2,048, 32,768, and 100,000 rows * 2 and 8 blocks * `float64`, mixed `float32`/`float64`, and `int64` blocks  At a significance factor of 1.05, 38 cases improved, 34 were unchanged, and none regressed. Statistically significant improvements ranged from approximately 8% to 60%.  Representative ASV results:  ```text sum, 100,000 rows, 8 float64 blocks: 2.15 ms -> 1.71 ms prod, 100,000 rows, 8 int64 blocks: 1.36 ms -> 0.547 ms min, 100,000 rows, 8 float64 blocks: 1.04 ms -> 0.487 ms max, 100,000 rows, 8 float64 blocks: 1.02 ms -> 0.498 ms ```  Matched ASV peak-memory measurements for 1,000,000 rows and eight `float64` blocks also improved:  ```text sum: 188 MB -> 175 MB min: 174 MB -> 158 MB ```  This is related to #51474 , the broader request to use `_reduce_axis1` for these reductions, and #65105, which implemented the multi-block fast path.  The issue described here is narrower: that fast path is already present, but it still materializes a per-block `middle` vector and an allocating combine result. titulo: PERF: avoid redundant allocations in StringArray duplicated and value_counts
corpo: ### Pandas version checks  - [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.  - [x] I have confirmed this issue exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.  - [x] I have confirmed this issue exists on the main branch of pandas.   ### Reproducible Example  ## Summary  Python-backed `StringArray` already stores its values in an object ndarray. However, `duplicated` and `value_counts(dropna=True)` currently perform avoidable allocations before hashing for arrays using `pd.NA`.  The two paths incur this overhead differently:  * `duplicated` already passes the existing backing ndarray through `_ensure_data` (`_ensure_data(arr) is arr._ndarray`), so it does not materialize another object ndarray. Its avoidable allocation is the boolean NA mask created by the generic extension-array path. * `value_counts(dropna=True)` creates a filtered object-array copy through boolean indexing before hashing.  For Python-backed `StringArray` using `pd.NA`, these allocations can be avoided by operating directly on the existing backing ndarray where the missing-value semantics permit it.  ## Proposed change  Use the existing backing ndarray directly when:  * The array is Python-backed. * Its missing-value sentinel is `pd.NA`. * For `value_counts`, `dropna=True`.  For `duplicated`, avoid constructing the generic NA mask when the backing ndarray can be hashed directly.  Retain the existing generic paths for other missing-value semantics, `dropna=False`, and other string backends.  This does not change public behavior or results.  ## Relation to #14860  This is related to #14860, which tracks improving `value_counts` and `duplicated` performance for string data through string-specific hashing.  This change is narrower. It removes avoidable allocations in the Python-backed `StringArray` dispatch path before hashing:  * A boolean NA mask for `duplicated`. * A filtered object-array copy for `value_counts(dropna=True)`.  It does not change the underlying hashtable implementation or introduce the general string-specific hashing approach discussed in #14860.  ## Benchmarks  ASV benchmarks used arrays containing 500,000 elements. Nullable cases replaced every tenth value with `pd.NA`, giving 10% missing values.  Among statistically significant comparisons:  * `duplicated`: 16/18 cases improved, 2 were unchanged, and none regressed. Significant improvements ranged from approximately 9% to 55%. * `value_counts`: 5/6 cases improved, 1 was unchanged, and none regressed. One no-null, cardinality-50,000 measurement had high variance and is omitted from the representative results.  Representative ASV results:  * `duplicated`, cardinality 256, no nulls, `keep="first"`:   **19.4 ± 0.03 ms → 8.76 ± 0.1 ms — 54.9% faster.** * `value_counts(dropna=True)`, cardinality 256, 10% nulls:   **31.3 ± 0.3 ms → 19.3 ± 0.08 ms — 38.2% faster.** * `value_counts(dropna=True)`, cardinality 50,000, 10% nulls:   **59.1 ± 0.3 ms → 45.2 ± 0.4 ms — 23.6% faster.** * `value_counts(dropna=True)`, cardinality 500,000, no nulls:   **322 ± 6 ms → 306 ± 3 ms — 4.7% faster.**  ## Reproducible timing example  ```python from timeit import repeat  import numpy as np import pandas as pd   def make_array(cardinality, has_nulls):     values = np.resize(         np.array([f"value-{i}" for i in range(cardinality)], dtype=object),         500_000,     )     if has_nulls:         values[::10] = pd.NA     return pd.array(         values,         dtype=pd.StringDtype(storage="python", na_value=pd.NA),     )   def best_ms(func):     return min(repeat(func, number=5, repeat=7)) / 5 * 1_000   no_nulls = make_array(256, False) nullable_256 = make_array(256, True) nullable_50k = make_array(50_000, True)  print("duplicated:", best_ms(lambda: no_nulls.duplicated(keep="first"))) print(     "value_counts 256:",     best_ms(lambda: nullable_256.value_counts(dropna=True)), ) print(     "value_counts 50k:",     best_ms(lambda: nullable_50k.value_counts(dropna=True)), ) ```  The script was run sequentially on upstream `main` and this branch. Units are milliseconds.  ```text upstream main baseline (4bcadf56): duplicated: 19.385 value_counts 256: 31.510 value_counts 50k: 56.471  this branch (4a78335a): duplicated: 8.960 value_counts 256: 20.346 value_counts 50k: 46.216 ```  The relevant upstream files have not changed since baseline commit `4bcadf56`.  ## Tests  Coverage has been implemented for:  * All `duplicated(keep=...)` modes. * Unicode and empty arrays. * Duplicate missing values. * Nullable and NumPy-style missing-value semantics. * Fast-path and fallback dispatch. * Existing string backends.    ## Automation disclosure  OpenAI Codex using gpt-5.6-sol with xhigh reasoning effort produced the initial runtime candidate. OpenAI Codex using Codex Sol 5.6 with reasoning effort set to max was used for subsequent development and validation.  ### Installed Versions    <details>  ```text INSTALLED VERSIONS ------------------ commit                : 4bcadf56f04581c607707ccefa547dc039d003f8 python                : 3.13.5 python-bits           : 64 OS                    : Linux OS-release            : 6.8.0-1060-aws Version               : #63~22.04.1-Ubuntu SMP Tue Jun 30 02:32:53 UTC 2026 machine               : x86_64 processor             : x86_64 byteorder             : little LC_ALL                : None LANG                  : C.UTF-8 LOCALE                : C.UTF-8  pandas                : 3.1.0.dev0+1740.g4bcadf56f0 numpy                 : 2.5.2 dateutil              : 2.9.0.post0 pip                   : 26.2.1 Cython                : 3.3.0 sphinx                : None IPython               : None adbc-driver-postgresql: None adbc-driver-sqlite    : None bs4                   : None bottleneck            : None fastparquet            : None fsspec                : None html5lib              : None gcsfs                 : None jinja2                : 3.1.6 lxml.etree            : None matplotlib            : 3.11.1 numba                 : 0.67.0 numexpr               : 2.14.2 odfpy                 : None openpyxl              : 3.1.5 psycopg2              : None pymysql               : None pyarrow               : 25.0.1 pyiceberg             : None pyreadstat            : None pytest                : None python-calamine       : None pytz                  : None pyxlsb                : None s3fs                  : None scipy                 : 1.18.1 sqlalchemy            : 2.0.52 tables                : 3.11.1 tabulate              : None xarray                : None xlrd                  : None xlsxwriter            : 3.2.9 zstandard             : None qtpy                  : None pyqt5                 : None ```     </details>  ### Prior Performance  NA

titulo: BUG: pd.to_numeric with errors="coerce" fails to produce actual NA values when applied to dtype string[pyarrow] values
corpo: ### Pandas version checks  - [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.  - [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.  - [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.   ### Reproducible Example  ```python import pandas as pd  df = pd.DataFrame(data={"A": ["1", "NaN"]}) df = df.convert_dtypes(dtype_backend="pyarrow") numeric = pd.to_numeric(df["A"], errors="coerce")  print(numeric) print("Not detected as NaN:") print(numeric.isna()) print("Forward fill doesn't fill:") print(numeric.ffill()) ```  ### Issue Description  When applying pd.to_numeric with ``errors="coerce"`` to a column with dtype string[pyarrow] and entries that are unable to be parsed, the resulting NaN values are not detected as such. This results for example in later issues when ``df.interpolate`` does not replace those missing values.  ### Expected Behavior  I would expect that errors="coerce" produces NaN values during pd.to_numeric, which are later detected via ``df.isna()`` and replaced during ``df.ffill()``. This is how the example above behaves for the numpy backend and I would expect the pyarrow backend to do the same.  ### Installed Versions  <details>  INSTALLED VERSIONS ------------------ commit                : e68db09ecf6427d1b62e565bacf17f2e525a3032 python                : 3.11.16 python-bits           : 64 OS                    : Windows OS-release            : 10 Version               : 10.0.22631 machine               : AMD64 processor             : Intel64 Family 6 Model 143 Stepping 8, GenuineIntel byteorder             : little LC_ALL                : None LANG                  : en_US.UTF-8 LOCALE                : English_United States.1252  pandas                : 3.0.5 numpy                 : 2.4.6 dateutil              : 2.9.0.post0 pip                   : 26.2.1 Cython                : None sphinx                : None IPython               : 9.16.1 adbc-driver-postgresql: None adbc-driver-sqlite    : None bs4                   : None bottleneck            : None fastparquet           : None fsspec                : None html5lib              : None hypothesis            : None gcsfs                 : None jinja2                : 3.1.6 lxml.etree            : 6.1.2 matplotlib            : 3.11.1 numba                 : None numexpr               : None odfpy                 : None openpyxl              : 3.1.5 psycopg2              : None pymysql               : None pyarrow               : 25.0.1 pyiceberg             : None pyreadstat            : None pytest                : 8.4.2 python-calamine       : None pytz                  : 2026.3.post1 pyxlsb                : 1.0.10 s3fs                  : None scipy                 : 1.17.1 sqlalchemy            : 2.0.52 tables                : None tabulate              : None xarray                : None xlrd                  : 2.0.2 xlsxwriter            : 3.2.9 zstandard             : None qtpy                  : None pyqt5                 : None None  </details>

titulo: API: Add reduction methods to ExtensionArray
corpo: This is a follow-up to #64450 which was implemented in #63512. The PR implemented reduction methods like `sum`, `min`, `mean`, ... for some internal EAs. It also implements the [`BaseReduceTests::test_reduce_array`](https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/964b99e97a9856a66fdec90f8eede7d9a6301324/pandas/tests/extension/base/reduce.py#L135) test function which expects that all EAs implement these methods but they are not part of the public EA API yet. The topic about adding these reduction methods to the API was discussed in the developer meeting on 2026-08-26 with the following opinions expressed by the participants: - Participants are on board for adding these - Some participants like the idea of following up by removing the `EA._reduce` indirection. There’s some concern about the deprecation path for that  At the moment the `_reduce` method by default already dispatches to the reduction methods if they are implemented: https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/964b99e97a9856a66fdec90f8eede7d9a6301324/pandas/core/arrays/base.py#L2478-L2483  From that a possible deprecation path could be to implement the reduction methods (raising `TypeError` or `NotImplemented` by default). However at the moment some of our internal EAs currently implement the functionality in `_reduce` and dispatch from the reduction methods to that, e.g. in `BaseMaskedArray`: https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/964b99e97a9856a66fdec90f8eede7d9a6301324/pandas/core/arrays/masked.py#L1840-L1843  Due to the current implementation of `_reduce` we cannot implement the base reduction methods like `BaseMaskedArray` to resolve to `_reduce` as that would create a `RecursionError`.  For external EAs that currently use a similar pattern to `BaseMaskedArray` that would mean that the `test_reduce_array` test currently still fails, because `self._supports_reduction` likely returns `True`, but `res_op = getattr(ser.array, op_name)` will raise the error specified in the base class. I think that would be okay, because then external EA developer are informed to implement / overwrite the base methods. Maybe there could be an additional comment in test notifying developers that `_reduce` will eventually be deprecated?  @rhshadrach @jbrockmendel Would welcome your feedback on the desired approach, implementation then should be relatively straight forward.

corpo: ### Pandas version checks  - [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.  - [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.  - [ ] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.   ### Reproducible Example  ```python import pandas as pd import matplotlib.pyplot as plt  df = pd.DataFrame(     {         'date': pd.to_datetime(             [                 '1979-01-01',                 '1979-04-01',                 '1979-07-01',                 '1979-10-01',                 '1980-01-01',                 '1980-04-01',             ]         ),         'gdp': [             2526.610,             2591.247,             2667.565,             2723.883,             2789.842,             2797.352,         ],     } )  colors = ['g', 'g', 'g', 'g', 'r', 'r']  print(df.dtypes) print('Frequency:', pd.DatetimeIndex(df['date']).freq) print('Inferred frequency:', pd.DatetimeIndex(df['date']).inferred_freq)  df.plot(     kind='bar',     x='date',     y='gdp',     color=colors,     rot=90, )  plt.show() ```  ### Issue Description  DataFrame.plot(kind='bar') raises:  ValueError: Must supply freq for datetime value  when a datetime64[us] column is supplied through x=.  The exception occurs inside pandas plotting code while BarPlot initializes PeriodConverter with data.index.freq. The DatetimeIndex has freq=None, although its frequency can be inferred as QS-OCT.  Relevant end of traceback:  File "pandas/plotting/_matplotlib/core.py", line 1877, in __init__     PeriodConverter.convert_from_freq(         self._get_xticks(),         data.index.freq,     ) File "pandas/plotting/_matplotlib/converter.py", line 245, in convert_from_freq     values = PeriodConverter._convert_1d(values, freq) File "pandas/plotting/_matplotlib/converter.py", line 281, in _get_datevalue     return Period(date, freq).ordinal ValueError: Must supply freq for datetime value  The same plotting operation works in another tested environment using:  - Python 3.12.11 - pandas 2.2.3 - Matplotlib 3.8.4 - date dtype datetime64[ns] - DatetimeIndex.freq is also None - DatetimeIndex.inferred_freq is QS-OCT  The failing environment uses:  - Python 3.13 - pandas 3.0.5 - Matplotlib 3.11.1 - date dtype datetime64[us]  The data itself can be plotted successfully by either:  1. converting the datetime values to strings before calling DataFrame.plot.bar; or 2. calling matplotlib.pyplot.bar directly with the original datetime values.  I confirmed that the issue reproduces in a fresh **Jupyter notebook** using the minimal standalone example, without reading external files or performing a merge.  This suggests a regression or compatibility issue in the pandas bar-plot datetime conversion path. titulo: BUG: IntervalDtype.__from_arrow__ ignores the struct-level validity bitmap
corpo: ### Reproducible Example  ```python import numpy as np import pandas as pd import pyarrow as pa  st = pa.struct([("left", pa.float64()), ("right", pa.float64())]) arr = pa.array([{"left": 0.0, "right": 1.0}, None], type=st) pd.IntervalDtype(np.dtype("float64"), "right").__from_arrow__(arr) # <IntervalArray> # [(0.0, 1.0], (0.0, 0.0]] # Length: 2, dtype: interval[float64, right] ```  ### Issue Description  The second entry is null in the arrow array but reads back as `(0.0, 0.0]` instead of NA.  `IntervalDtype.__from_arrow__` reads only `arr.field("left")` / `arr.field("right")`. pyarrow's `StructArray.field()` does not merge the parent struct's validity bitmap into the child, so a null struct entry whose children are non-null is read as whatever the children hold (typically 0).  This is not reachable from pandas-written data: `IntervalArray.__arrow_array__` nulls both the child values and the struct-level bitmap, so `np.asarray(child)` recovers the NaN. Only externally-produced arrow data trips it.  The fix is to apply `arr.is_valid()` (or use `arr.flatten()`, which does apply the parent bitmap) before building the `IntervalArray`.  Found while working on GH-64297.  ### Expected Behavior  The second interval is NA.

titulo: BUG: IntervalArray.__arrow_array__ rejects ExtensionDtype subtypes, and ArrowIntervalType metadata cannot round-trip them
corpo: ### Reproducible Example  ```python import pandas as pd import pyarrow as pa  ser = pd.Series(pd.IntervalIndex.from_breaks(pd.date_range("2012", periods=5, tz="Europe/Brussels"))) pa.array(ser) # TypeError: Conversion to arrow with subtype 'datetime64[us, Europe/Brussels]' is not supported ```  ### Issue Description  `IntervalArray.__arrow_array__` computes the arrow subtype with `pyarrow.from_numpy_dtype(self.dtype.subtype)`, which raises for any `ExtensionDtype` subtype — including `DatetimeTZDtype`, which `IntervalArray` otherwise supports.  GH-64297 fixed only the read side (`IntervalDtype.__from_arrow__`), so an interval-with-tz column can now be read from arrow but still cannot be written.  Lifting the restriction is not just a subtype-lookup change: `ArrowIntervalType.__arrow_ext_serialize__` stores `str(self.subtype)` and deserializes with `pyarrow.type_for_alias`, which has no alias for `timestamp[us, tz=Europe/Brussels]`. Simply allowing the write produces parquet that fails to read back:  ``` ValueError: No type alias for timestamp[us, tz=europe/brussels] ```  So a fix needs a metadata-format change on the registered `pandas.interval` extension type, which has cross-implementation compatibility implications and seems worth its own discussion.  ### Expected Behavior  `pa.array(ser)` succeeds for a tz-aware interval subtype, and the result round-trips through parquet back to the same `IntervalDtype`.
